cards.summary: Augustus gained control of Rome and its lands more than two thousand years ago. Rome’s empire stretched across large parts of Europe, western Asia, and northern Africa.

cards.title: How did Sacagawea help the Lewis and Clark expedition?
cards.summary: Sacagawea traveled with the group led by Lewis and Clark while carrying her young child. She could speak languages that helped the explorers communicate.

cards.title: How did sand dunes grow beside Lake Michigan?
cards.summary: Waves move sand along the Indiana shore of Lake Michigan. When sand dries on the beach, wind can pick up the loose grains and carry them farther inland.

cards.title: How did Sequoyah make a way to write Cherokee?
cards.summary: Sequoyah developed signs to write the Cherokee language. Most of the signs let a reader recognize a spoken syllable at a time.

cards.title: How did Spitzer see through some clouds of space dust?
cards.summary: Spitzer was a NASA space telescope that collected infrared light, which human eyes cannot see. Some infrared light gets through dust that can hide stars from an ordinary telescope.

cards.title: How did such a long inlet form in Washington?
cards.summary: Puget Sound is a long network of inlets in western Washington, connected to seawater from the Pacific Ocean. During a recent ice age, a large sheet of ice moved through the area.

cards.title: How did the ancient Maya organize their cities?
cards.summary: Ancient Maya people built cities across parts of what are now Mexico and Central America. Each city and the lands around it could have its own ruler.

cards.title: How did the ancient Persian Empire govern faraway lands?
cards.summary: The Achaemenid kings ruled an empire that stretched from Egypt and western Asia toward the Indus region. A king could not visit every town to decide what should happen there.

cards.title: How did the electric telegraph send words down a wire?
cards.summary: People used an electric telegraph to send messages between places joined by a wire. At one end, an operator pressed a key to turn the signal on and off.

cards.title: How did the Erie Canal move boats across New York?
cards.summary: Before railroads reached many places, the Erie Canal let boats carry goods between the Hudson River and Lake Erie. Crews dug long channels and built gates that could close off a section.

cards.title: How did the Inca rule across the Andes?
cards.summary: The Inca Empire stretched along the Andes of western South America before Spanish conquest. Its rulers governed from Cusco and linked many communities with roads.

cards.title: How did the Mississippi build land near the Gulf?
cards.summary: As the Mississippi River slows near the Gulf Coast, some of the sand and mud in the water settles out. Over time these deposits can build low new land between the channels.

cards.title: How did the modern Olympic Games begin?
cards.summary: The first modern Olympic Games opened in Athens, Greece, in 1896. Organizers drew inspiration from games held long before at Olympia.

cards.title: How did the Mongol Empire connect distant places?
cards.summary: Chinggis Khan united many groups on the grasslands of Inner Asia early in the thirteenth century. He and the rulers who followed him took control of lands far beyond those grasslands.

cards.title: How did the Nineteenth Amendment change voting?
cards.summary: The Nineteenth Amendment says that a U.S. citizen’s right to vote cannot be denied because of their sex.

cards.title: How did the Panama Canal change ocean travel?
cards.summary: Before the Panama Canal opened, ships traveling between the Atlantic and Pacific sides of the Americas often had to sail far around South America. Workers in Panama dug through hills, built dams, and made locks to raise ships to a lake and lower them again.

cards.title: How did the Qin form one Chinese empire?
cards.summary: Before the Qin empire, several powerful states competed for land in China. The Qin ruler defeated the others and called himself the First Emperor in 221 BCE.

cards.title: How did the Rosetta Stone help people read hieroglyphs?
cards.summary: The Rosetta Stone has the same announcement carved in three kinds of writing. One is in Greek, which scholars could already read.

cards.title: How did the Thirteenth Amendment change the Constitution?
cards.summary: The Thirteenth Amendment ended slavery and forced labor across the United States, except as punishment after conviction for a crime. States approved it in 1865, when the Civil War was ending.

cards.title: How did thirteen colonies become a new country?
cards.summary: The thirteen British colonies on the Atlantic coast included people who disagreed about who should make laws and collect taxes. Protest turned into fighting in 1775.

cards.title: How did towns of the Swahili coast trade across the ocean?
cards.summary: For centuries, merchants from towns along the eastern coast of Africa traded across the Indian Ocean. Sailors learned when winds were likely to carry boats toward Africa or away from it.

cards.title: How did trade help the Mali Empire grow?
cards.summary: The Mali Empire grew in West Africa along routes that linked regions with very different useful goods. Gold came from parts of West Africa, and salt could be brought from mines in the Sahara.

cards.title: How did two twin rovers find signs that Mars had once been wet?
cards.summary: Spirit and Opportunity reached opposite parts of Mars in 2004. They studied features in rocks and soil that could tell a story about water long ago.

cards.title: How did water build natural dams at Plitvice Lakes?
cards.summary: At Plitvice Lakes in Croatia, water runs from lake to lake over a series of waterfalls. It picks up dissolved minerals when it flows over and through some kinds of rock.

cards.title: How did water shape the city of Angkor?
cards.summary: Angkor grew in a part of Southeast Asia where rain changes greatly between seasons. Khmer builders made channels and wide places that could hold water.

cards.title: How did wind help build Iowa’s Loess Hills?
cards.summary: Along the Missouri River valley in western Iowa stand hills built of very small grains of soil called loess. During cold periods, water from melting ice carried fine bits of rock into wide river valleys.

cards.title: How did workers connect rail lines across the United States?
cards.summary: In the 1860s, the Central Pacific built tracks east from California while the Union Pacific built west from the middle of the country. Workers cut paths, moved earth, laid rails, and carried heavy equipment across mountains and plains.

cards.title: How do a story’s events make a plot?
cards.summary: A plot is the set of events that make up a story and the ways they fit together. Imagine someone loses a lunchbox, checks the classroom, follows a clue, and finds it on the soccer field.

cards.title: How do airplane wings and tails steer?
cards.summary: An airplane can point its nose up or down, turn it left or right, or tip one wing lower than the other. Moving parts push on flowing air to help make these turns.

cards.title: How do Arabic letters change shape in a word?
cards.summary: Arabic writing usually runs from right to left. Many letters join their neighbors, so a letter may look somewhat different at the beginning, middle, or end of a word.

cards.title: How do Bangla letters show which vowel to say?
cards.summary: Bangla, also called Bengali, is often written with letters that show a consonant plus a usual vowel. A reader can see other vowel sounds marked around that letter in different places.

cards.title: How do bars show data?
cards.summary: A bar graph uses bars to show how much is in each group. Imagine surveying a class about favorite fruit.

cards.title: How do California mussels stick to a rocky shore?
cards.summary: A California mussel makes strong threads that fasten its shell to a rock or to other mussels. Waves can pull hard on the shell without sweeping it away.

cards.title: How do capillaries deliver oxygen to cells?
cards.summary: The larger blood vessels branch into tiny tubes called capillaries. Each tube has a very thin wall.

cards.title: How do chromosomes help pack DNA?
cards.summary: DNA is long and thin, and a cell is tiny. To pack DNA into that small space, the cell winds it around proteins and folds it further.

cards.title: How do comic panels tell a story?
cards.summary: A comic tells a story with pictures and sometimes words. Pictures can sit in separate boxes called panels.

cards.title: How do computers agree which letters to show?
cards.summary: A text program needs a shared way to know which letter or sign a stored number means. Unicode assigns a number to a letter, sign, or other text character.

cards.title: How do computers keep files without power?
cards.summary: A computer keeps some information in devices that are built to remember without power. They can hold drawings, recordings, and programs between uses.

cards.title: How do dominoes fit into a chain?
cards.summary: A domino is a tile marked into two halves. Each half can have dots or be blank.

cards.title: How do Egyptian hieroglyphs work?
cards.summary: Ancient Egyptian hieroglyphs are signs used to write the Egyptian language. Some are easy to recognize as pictures, such as an owl or an eye.

cards.title: How do evergreen trees stay green all year?
cards.summary: Evergreen plants keep some green leaves throughout the year. That does not mean that each leaf lasts forever.

cards.title: How do farmers water crops when it does not rain?
cards.summary: Irrigation means bringing water to a place where plants need it. A farm may get water from a river, a well, or a place where water has been stored.

cards.title: How do folders help you find files?
cards.summary: If all of your saved work were in one big pile, it could be hard to find a particular drawing. A folder lets you give a name to a group of files.

cards.title: How do fresh and salty water meet in Chesapeake Bay?
cards.summary: Chesapeake Bay reaches inland from the Atlantic Ocean between land in Maryland and Virginia. Rivers bring fresh water into the bay.

cards.title: How do fungi help a fallen log break down?
cards.summary: A fallen branch still has food materials locked inside its tough wood. Some fungi grow into the branch and release substances that break the wood down.

cards.title: How do groups of cells do bigger jobs?
cards.summary: A single cell can send a message, move, or carry a supply, but a large body needs many cells working in groups. A group of organized cells and the material around them forms a tissue.

cards.title: How do ice crystals grow on a window?
cards.summary: Frost can form when moist air touches a surface that is cold enough for water to turn directly from vapor into ice. The new ice can grow in delicate branches across a window or along a blade of grass.

cards.title: How do joints let your body move?
cards.summary: A joint is a place where bones meet. Many joints let one bone move against the other.

cards.title: How do kitchen tongs pinch food without touching it with your hands?
cards.summary: A common pair of kitchen tongs has two long arms joined at one end. The ends far from the join can grip a piece of food.

cards.title: How do leaves help a plant grow?
cards.summary: Leaves give many plants a wide surface to catch sunlight. A green leaf uses light, water and a gas from the air to make sugars.

cards.title: How do lungs get oxygen into your body?
cards.summary: When you breathe in, air travels down your windpipe and through branches that get smaller and smaller inside your lungs. At the ends of many branches are clusters of tiny air sacs.

cards.title: How do many electronic parts fit on a single chip?
cards.summary: An integrated circuit puts many tiny electronic parts on one piece of material. The parts can include transistors and very small tracks that join them.

cards.title: How do masonry workers build with blocks, brick, or stone?
cards.summary: Masonry workers build with pieces such as brick, stone, and concrete blocks. A bricklayer follows a plan and uses tools to keep each row even and the wall upright.

cards.title: How do meters, centimeters, and kilometers fit together?
cards.summary: A meter is a unit of length. A centimeter is one hundredth of a meter, so a meter stick has a hundred centimeters along it.

cards.title: How do muscles move your bones?
cards.summary: When you bend your elbow, muscles near your upper arm put a pull on your bones. Strong strips called tendons attach many muscles to bones.

cards.title: How do musicians know how loudly to play?
cards.summary: Dynamics tell musicians how loud or soft their music should sound. A group may begin so softly that you can barely hear it, then grow louder until the whole room seems full.

cards.title: How do number lines show where numbers belong?
cards.summary: A number line puts numbers in order and shows how far apart they are. On the usual horizontal line, numbers get larger as you move right.

cards.title: How do orchestra musicians play together?
cards.summary: An orchestra is a group of musicians who play different instruments together. A typical orchestra includes strings, woodwinds, brass, and percussion.

cards.title: How do people learn a traditional craft?
cards.summary: Someone learning a traditional craft can watch a person who already knows the work, try a step, and ask what to change. A basket maker might show a learner which plants bend without snapping.

cards.title: How do people read braille?
cards.summary: Braille uses patterns of raised dots. A reader feels them with their fingertips.

cards.title: How do pine trees grow in the sandy Pinelands?
cards.summary: The Pinelands lie on southern New Jersey’s low coastal plain. Much of their soil is sandy, so water drains through it more easily than it does through sticky clay.

cards.title: How do plants grow below a shady forest canopy?
cards.summary: Shrubs, young trees, and some small plants grow below the tallest trees. This part of the forest is the understory.

cards.title: How do prairie plants grow back after a fire?
cards.summary: In many tallgrass prairies, fires can burn dry stems without destroying every growing part of the grasses. Buds near or below the soil surface can survive and send up fresh shoots.

cards.title: How do programmers find and fix bugs?
cards.summary: A bug is a problem in a program. Imagine a score that goes up when the player should lose a point.

cards.title: How do red blood cells carry oxygen?
cards.summary: A red blood cell is a flexible, flat disc with thinner spots in its middle. It carries a substance called hemoglobin.

cards.title: How do researchers recognize a right whale?
cards.summary: A North Atlantic right whale has patches of rough skin on its head. Tiny animals live on those raised spots and can make them look white.

cards.title: How do rows help you multiply?
cards.summary: Imagine setting out three rows of four buttons. Each row has the same number, so you can count by fours or multiply three by four.

cards.title: How do savannas have trees and grass in the same place?
cards.summary: A tropical savanna has grasses with trees or shrubs scattered among them. Many savannas have a rainy season followed by a dry one.

cards.title: How do scraps turn into compost?
cards.summary: A compost pile gives little animals and other living things a place to break down dead leaves, plant scraps and similar materials. They use some parts as food.

cards.title: How do screens mix red, green, and blue light?
cards.summary: Many screens create colors by mixing red, green, and blue light. A little spot on the screen can get a different amount of each color.

cards.title: How do seeds get far from the parent plant?
cards.summary: A seed often has a better chance to find space and light if it lands away from its parent. A dandelion makes tiny dry fruits that float in the breeze on little parachutes.

cards.title: How do shipping containers move from a ship to land?
cards.summary: Large boxes called shipping containers can ride on a ship, railroad car, or truck. At a port, a tall crane can lift a box from the ship, carry it over the dock, and lower it onto a waiting area or vehicle.

cards.title: How do snowplows make a path along a street?
cards.summary: A snowplow uses a wide blade to push snow out of a travel path. Moving the snow creates a clearer path for the next vehicle, but the snow is still somewhere nearby.

cards.title: How do stones surround space in Go?
cards.summary: Go is a board game in which two players take turns putting black and white stones where lines cross. Once a stone is placed, it stays there unless it is captured.

cards.title: How do taste buds tell flavors apart?
cards.summary: When you take a bite, tiny bits of dissolved food meet taste cells. Groups of such cells form taste buds.

cards.title: How do the faces of a box fit together?
cards.summary: A rectangular box has six flat faces. Each face meets its neighbor along an edge, and three edges come together at a corner.

cards.title: How do the greater-than and less-than signs work?
cards.summary: The wide opening faces the greater number and the point faces the smaller one. In 4 < 9, the opening faces nine, so read it as four is less than nine.

cards.title: How do tiny fibers become a sheet of paper?
cards.summary: Many kinds of paper start with tiny wood fibers. A mill separates the fibers and mixes them with water, making a wet mass called pulp.

cards.title: How do train wheels follow a curve in the tracks?
cards.summary: Many train wheels become a little narrower in diameter toward their outside edge. On a curve, a wheel and its partner can shift sideways on the rails.

cards.title: How do trees live in the northern boreal forest?
cards.summary: Across much of northern North America and Eurasia lies a great stretch of forest called the boreal forest, or taiga. Winters are long and cold there.

cards.title: How do watercolors make light colors?
cards.summary: With watercolors, a brush carries small bits of color mixed with water. A thin layer lets light reach the white paper and bounce back, so the paper helps the color look bright or pale.

cards.title: How do we know about the Shang dynasty?
cards.summary: The Shang dynasty ruled parts of northern China more than three thousand years ago. Its craftspeople made large bronze containers with carefully shaped patterns.

cards.title: How do wheat kernels turn into flour?
cards.summary: Wheat plants make dry kernels. A mill breaks the kernels into pieces and can sift the pieces by how big they are.

cards.title: How do white spruce cones hang on the tree?
cards.summary: A white spruce carries its seed cones below the branches like small hanging decorations. They are narrow and have thin scales.

cards.title: How do written notes tell us what to play?
cards.summary: Written music gives performers a set of marks to follow. In a familiar kind of musical notation, notes sit on or between five lines called a staff.

cards.title: How do you add fractions with different bottom numbers?
cards.summary: First rewrite the fractions so their pieces are the same size. To add one half and one quarter, imagine two matching paper circles.

cards.title: How do you add fractions with the same bottom number?
cards.summary: When two fractions describe equal-sized pieces, count how many pieces you have in all. One fifth plus two fifths gives three fifths.

cards.title: How do you feel rough and smooth things?
cards.summary: Try brushing a finger over paper, a sweater, or the top of a table. The push on the skin changes as your finger travels over tiny bumps.

cards.title: How do you find one point on a grid?
cards.summary: On a simple grid, start where the two number lines meet. The first number in an ordered pair tells you where to go sideways.

cards.title: How do you find the median?
cards.summary: Put the numbers 2, 6, 7, 10, and 50 in order from smallest to largest. The number in the middle is seven.

cards.title: How do you flip a shape across a line?
cards.summary: A flip, or reflection, puts each point of a shape at a matching spot across a line. Hold a mirror upright on a drawn line and the picture in the mirror shows the idea.

cards.title: How do you get to know a story character?
cards.summary: A character is a person, animal, or other being who takes part in a story. You can learn about one by watching what they do, hearing what they say, and noticing what other characters think about them.

cards.title: How do you measure area?
cards.summary: Area tells how much flat space a shape covers. Picture a rectangle made of square tiles that all have the same size.

cards.title: How do you measure around a shape?
cards.summary: The perimeter is the distance all the way around a flat shape. Picture a rectangular garden that is six steps long and four steps wide.

cards.title: How do you measure the space inside a box?
cards.summary: Volume tells you how much three-dimensional space something takes up. Imagine fitting small cubes into a rectangular box.

cards.title: How do you read the hands on a clock?
cards.summary: On many clocks, the short hand shows the hour and the long hand shows the minutes. When the long hand points at the twelve, it is at the start of an hour.

cards.title: How do you round a number?
cards.summary: Rounding replaces a number with a nearby number that is easier to say or use. To round 47 to the nearest ten, look at 40 and 50.

cards.title: How do you score in soccer?
cards.summary: In soccer, two teams try to get the ball into the other team’s goal. A goal counts when the whole ball goes over the goal line between the posts and under the crossbar, as long as the scoring team has not broken a rule.

cards.title: How do you smell something nearby?
cards.summary: A bowl of cut oranges can smell fresh from across a table. Some molecules leave the fruit and move through the air.

cards.title: How do you turn a fraction into a decimal?
cards.summary: A fraction bar can stand for division. To write three fourths as a decimal, divide three by four.

cards.title: How do your ears hear?
cards.summary: A sound sends vibrations through the air. When those vibrations reach your ear, they make a thin part called the eardrum move.

cards.title: How do your eyes help you see?
cards.summary: Light from the world enters your eye through a round opening. Clear parts near the front bend the light so it makes a sharp picture on a layer at the back.

cards.title: How do your fingernails grow?
cards.summary: Your fingernail grows from a group of cells under the skin near the base of the nail. These cells make new nail material that slowly pushes older nail forward.

cards.title: How does a Baltimore oriole hang its nest from thin branches?
cards.summary: A Baltimore oriole makes a hanging nest that can look like a small cloth bag. The female works narrow strands around twigs and around other strands.

cards.title: How does a barnacle live stuck to a rock?
cards.summary: An acorn barnacle starts life swimming in the sea. Later it settles on a hard surface and sticks there.

cards.title: How does a barrier island shelter a coast?
cards.summary: A barrier island is a long, usually narrow island that runs near and roughly along a coast. Ocean waves hit its outer beach first.

cards.title: How does a bend in a river become a lake?
cards.summary: As a winding river flows, it can wear away the outside banks of one bend. The two ends of that bend can slowly get closer.

cards.title: How does a bicycle chain carry your push to the back wheel?
cards.summary: When you press a bicycle pedal, you turn a ring with teeth near your feet. The teeth catch the links of the chain and pull it around.

cards.title: How does a bicycle pump make air go into a tire?
cards.summary: A bicycle pump has a moving piece called a piston that fits inside a tube. Pushing the handle moves the piston and squeezes the air in front of it.

cards.title: How does a bloodroot flower rise from the woods in spring?
cards.summary: A bloodroot flower can begin rising from the ground tucked inside the sides of a folded leaf. The leaf partly wraps around the young flower.

cards.title: How does a bog build up peat?
cards.summary: In many bogs, rain and snow supply most of the water. Peat moss and other plants grow on top of a thick layer of soaked plant remains called peat.

cards.title: How does a bottlenose dolphin find a fish in murky water?
cards.summary: A bottlenose dolphin can see in the water, but it has another way to find food in poor light. It makes short clicks and listens for echoes that bounce back from nearby objects.

cards.title: How does a box turtle shut the opening in its shell?
cards.summary: An eastern box turtle can draw its head, tail, and feet into its shell when danger is close. Underneath the turtle is a movable joint called a shell hinge.

cards.title: How does a budget help you plan?
cards.summary: A budget is a plan for using money. Imagine you expect to have twelve dollars this month.

cards.title: How does a cacao seed become chocolate?
cards.summary: Making chocolate begins with cacao seeds surrounded by pulp. Changes during fermentation help develop the flavors.

cards.title: How does a call number show where a library book goes?
cards.summary: A call number is a group of numbers or letters a library puts on a book so people can find its place. Some parts can group books on similar subjects, and other parts help sort books within that group.

cards.title: How does a can opener run its little cutting wheel around a can?
cards.summary: A hand can opener can have two small wheels near each other. The rough wheel grips the rim of the can.

cards.title: How does a chain pickerel hide while it waits for food?
cards.summary: A chain pickerel can wait in or near water plants with most of its long body barely moving. If a small fish swims within reach, the pickerel can dart forward.

cards.title: How does a checkout know the price when it scans a box?
cards.summary: In many shops the code on a package tells the checkout which product the shopper brought. The checkout can look up that item in the store’s records and get the price from there.

cards.title: How does a chickadee save food for later?
cards.summary: A black-capped chickadee can take one seed and fly off to tuck it away in a small hiding place. It may hide food in many separate spots, such as cracks in bark.

cards.title: How does a city bus driver keep track of a route?
cards.summary: A public bus driver carries people along a route with set stops. The driver watches the road and the people arriving at each stop, and works to keep the bus close to its schedule.

cards.title: How does a classroom aide help a teacher?
cards.summary: A classroom aide, or teacher assistant, helps pupils practice and helps the teacher run the room. During a lesson, an aide might work with a small group that needs more time with the same idea.

cards.title: How does a clothes dryer get water out of wet clothes?
cards.summary: A tumble dryer turns a big drum so wet clothes keep lifting and falling. This spreads them out and brings moving air to many parts of the cloth.

cards.title: How does a computer mouse tell which way it moved?
cards.summary: An optical mouse shines light onto the surface beneath it. A tiny sensor makes images of that small patch again and again.

cards.title: How does a dandelion pull off its parachute trick?
cards.summary: The yellow head on a common dandelion is made from many small flowers. Later it can become a white ball filled with what look like tiny parachutes.

cards.title: How does a database help find a record?
cards.summary: A database is an organized store of information that a program can look through. A class library’s database might store one record for every book.

cards.title: How does a dishwasher reach the dishes on both racks?
cards.summary: A dishwasher sends water through small holes in spray arms. The jets help spin the arms, sweeping water across the plates, bowls, and cups.

cards.title: How does a factor tree break a number into primes?
cards.summary: A factor tree starts with a number and splits it into two smaller factors greater than one. Start with 36 and split it into six times six.

cards.title: How does a flute make a sound without a reed?
cards.summary: A flute player blows a thin stream of air across an opening near one end. The air meets a sharp edge and sets the air inside the instrument moving back and forth.

cards.title: How does a giant anteater eat without teeth?
cards.summary: A giant anteater has a long, narrow face and no teeth. When it finds an ant or termite nest, it can rake open a small spot with its front claws.

cards.title: How does a giant manta ray eat tiny food?
cards.summary: A giant manta has wide fins that look like wings as it glides through the sea. Small flaps at the front of its head help guide water into its open mouth.

cards.title: How does a guitar change notes?
cards.summary: A guitar string makes a sound when you pluck it and it vibrates. On an acoustic guitar, those vibrations move into the body, which helps spread the sound.

cards.title: How does a hinge let a door turn without falling away?
cards.summary: One flat part of a common hinge attaches to the door, and another attaches to the frame. Little rounded sections on the two parts fit between one another.

cards.title: How does a hole become a natural rock arch?
cards.summary: In places such as Arches National Park, cracks split sandstone into long, narrow walls. Rain can get into cracks, and pieces of rock gradually break and fall away.

cards.title: How does a jet airplane slow down on a runway?
cards.summary: A passenger jet may use several things to slow down on the runway. Brakes act on some wheels as they roll.

cards.title: How does a land surveyor measure a place?
cards.summary: A land surveyor measures the positions of points on the ground. Pretend a path is going to cross a hill where no street signs mark the way.

cards.title: How does a letter carrier bring many people their mail?
cards.summary: A letter carrier delivers mail to addresses along a route. The carrier needs the right letters and packages for each stop, and may take outgoing mail from places along the way.

cards.title: How does a letter-and-number grid help you find a place?
cards.summary: A map grid divides a map into little squares. A row or column of letters and a row or column of numbers can give each square a name, such as B3.

cards.title: How does a lever make a job easier?
cards.summary: A lever is a stiff piece that turns around a fixed point. A seesaw is a lever, and the support under its middle is the turning point, called a fulcrum.

cards.title: How does a library catalog help you find a book?
cards.summary: A library catalog is a list of the things a library keeps, with details that help you find them. You can look up a title that you remember, search for an author you like, or try a topic, such as oceans.

cards.title: How does a library turn an old book into a digital copy?
cards.summary: A person making a digital copy of a book may use a camera or a scanner to capture images of its pages. The staff checks whether the words and pictures can be seen clearly and whether all pages are there in the right order.

cards.title: How does a limpet hold on to a rock?
cards.summary: A limpet is a sea snail with a shell shaped a little like a low hat. A broad, muscular foot spreads under it.

cards.title: How does a local delivery driver handle many stops?
cards.summary: A local delivery driver might start with many packages going to different places. The order of the stops matters because going back and forth across town wastes time.

cards.title: How does a machinist make a part the exact size it needs to be?
cards.summary: A machinist makes parts that need exact shapes and sizes. A drawing can show whether a part needs a hole, a flat face, or a certain width.

cards.title: How does a mechanical pencil feed out more graphite?
cards.summary: In many mechanical pencils, small jaws grip a thin stick of graphite, the material that leaves the gray mark. Pressing the button shifts the jaws and moves the stick forward a little.

cards.title: How does a meteorologist put together a weather forecast?
cards.summary: A meteorologist studies weather and uses clues to forecast what may happen next. A forecaster can look at readings near the ground and at pictures of clouds from space.

cards.title: How does a microwave oven heat food?
cards.summary: A microwave oven makes a kind of wave that carries energy into food. It can make certain molecules in the food, including water molecules, move in ways that warm the food.

cards.title: How does a museum keep track of each object?
cards.summary: A museum can keep a record for each object showing what it is, where it came from if that is known, and where it is now. Staff give the object a number or code that connects it with that record.

cards.title: How does a number machine work?
cards.summary: A number machine is a way to picture a rule. Put in a number, follow the same rule each time, and see what number comes out.

cards.title: How does a nuthatch look for food going down a tree?
cards.summary: A white-breasted nuthatch can grip the rough surface of a tree and head straight down with its beak first. The bird stops to check gaps in the bark for food.

cards.title: How does a pitcher plant catch insects?
cards.summary: Some pitcher plants make hollow leaves shaped like deep cups. An insect can slip inside and find it hard to climb out.

cards.title: How does a plant send sugar to its roots?
cards.summary: A leaf might make more sugar than it needs right away. The plant can send some of that sugar to other places through a tissue called phloem.

cards.title: How does a plant spread by underground stems?
cards.summary: A rhizome is a stem that grows sideways, often just below the ground. Roots can grow down from it.

cards.title: How does a protractor measure a turn?
cards.summary: A protractor is a tool with numbers marked around part of a circle. Put its center on the point where the two sides of an angle meet, and line its zero mark up with one side.

cards.title: How does a proverb say a lot in a few words?
cards.summary: A proverb is a short saying that people repeat to share an idea or some advice. For example, “Many hands make light work” tells us that a big job can feel easier when more people help.

cards.title: How does a pulley help lift something?
cards.summary: A pulley is a wheel with a groove that guides a rope or cable. Hang one pulley from a support, run a rope over it, and tie a load to one end.

cards.title: How does a raccoon use its front paws?
cards.summary: A raccoon has five long toes on each front paw. It can use the toes to turn food around, feel along the ground, and pick up small things.

cards.title: How does a red fox catch prey it cannot see?
cards.summary: A mouse can move under grass or snow without showing itself. A red fox may stop, tilt its head, and listen.

cards.title: How does a refrigerator move heat out of its cold space?
cards.summary: A refrigerator uses a fluid that flows through tubes in a loop. In the cold part of the loop, some of the fluid turns into gas and takes in heat from inside the refrigerator.

cards.title: How does a relay team pass a baton at speed?
cards.summary: In a track relay, each runner races part of the distance and hands a short baton to the next member of the team. The next runner may start moving before the baton arrives so both runners are going quickly during the handoff.

cards.title: How does a reporter find out what happened?
cards.summary: A reporter gathers information about events and explains it to readers, listeners, or viewers. The work can include visiting a place, asking people questions, and reading records.

cards.title: How does a rice cooker notice when the water is nearly gone?
cards.summary: A rice cooker can watch the temperature of its pot. While water is boiling, it takes in a lot of heat as some of it turns to steam.

cards.title: How does a road crossing warn that a train is coming?
cards.summary: At some crossings, a road and railway meet without a bridge between them. A busy crossing may have flashing lights, bells, and gates that move down when a train approaches.

cards.title: How does a root know which way is down?
cards.summary: A root does not need to see the ground to grow down into it. Certain cells near many root tips can detect the direction of gravity.

cards.title: How does a router pass a message between networks?
cards.summary: A router joins networks and helps information travel between them. When a packet comes in, router equipment looks at where it is headed.

cards.title: How does a saguaro cactus keep water inside?
cards.summary: Look at a saguaro and you can see long folds down its green stem. They let the stem swell when the cactus takes in water and draw in as it uses that stored water.

cards.title: How does a saguaro cactus save water?
cards.summary: A saguaro has a tall, green stem with folds along its sides. It can store water in that stem when rain is available.

cards.title: How does a script tell actors what to do?
cards.summary: A play script gives actors the words to speak and clues about what to do onstage. It may put each character’s name before their lines.

cards.title: How does a sea anemone catch food?
cards.summary: A sea anemone can look like a flower, with a ring of soft tentacles around the center. It is an animal that eats other animals.

cards.title: How does a sea lion walk on a beach?
cards.summary: A California sea lion can turn its back flippers forward and use them to walk on land. That makes it easier to move around on a beach or a rocky shore.

cards.title: How does a search engine find pages?
cards.summary: A search engine can find pages ahead of time and build a list of clues about them. That list is often called an index.

cards.title: How does a seed wake up and grow?
cards.summary: A dry seed can hold a tiny plant and its food supply for a long time. When conditions fit what that kind of plant needs, the seed takes in water and swells.

cards.title: How does a sewing machine join two threads to make a stitch?
cards.summary: A common sewing machine uses one thread from above and another from a small spool below the cloth. The needle carries the upper thread down and then starts back up, leaving a loop.

cards.title: How does a small tug help move a big ship?
cards.summary: A cargo ship can travel far across the open sea, but moving it sideways near a dock can be hard. One or more tugboats can help by pushing against its side or pulling through a strong line.

cards.title: How does a speaker turn electric signals into sound?
cards.summary: In a common loudspeaker, an electric signal passes through a coil of wire near a magnet. Their pushes and pulls make the coil move.

cards.title: How does a strawberry plant make a runner?
cards.summary: A strawberry plant can stretch a long, thin stem across the soil. The stem is called a runner.

cards.title: How does a striped skunk give a warning?
cards.summary: A striped skunk often tries to make a threat back away before using its strong-smelling spray. It can stamp its front feet and lift its tail.

cards.title: How does a summer thunderstorm make ice?
cards.summary: A thunderstorm can send a strong stream of air upward. Water droplets often stay liquid even when they are below their usual freezing temperature.

cards.title: How does a team score runs in cricket?
cards.summary: Cricket has two ends of a long strip called the pitch. A batter stands near each end.

cards.title: How does a tennis rally work?
cards.summary: A tennis point starts with a serve. The player hits the ball toward the correct service box across the net.

cards.title: How does a thermostat know when to stop heating?
cards.summary: A thermostat compares the temperature it measures with the temperature people have set. When the room grows cooler than the setting, the thermostat can tell a heater to start.

cards.title: How does a toilet flush and fill again?
cards.summary: In many toilets, pressing the handle lets water rush from a tank into the bowl. The fast flow can fill a curved passage and start drawing water from the bowl down the drain.

cards.title: How does a tracking page know where a package has been?
cards.summary: A package that can be tracked has a number that connects it to a set of records. Machines or workers can scan its label at different stops.

cards.title: How does a trumpet make different notes?
cards.summary: A trumpet player presses their lips to a small mouthpiece and blows so the lips buzz. The air inside the trumpet moves with the buzz.

cards.title: How does a trumpet vine hang on while it climbs?
cards.summary: A trumpet vine can hold onto rough bark or another solid surface with little roots growing out of the stem. The small roots reach into rough spots and help support the vine as it grows.

cards.title: How does a two-toed sloth live upside down?
cards.summary: A two-toed sloth can spend hours hanging from branches in a tropical forest. Its long, curved claws hook over a branch like handles, and strong limbs help hold it in place.

cards.title: How does a Venus flytrap catch a fly?
cards.summary: A Venus flytrap has hinged leaves with tiny hairs on their inside surfaces. When a small insect moves around and brushes the right hairs within a short time, a leaf can snap closed.

cards.title: How does a violin make a sound?
cards.summary: A violin player draws a bow across a string to make it vibrate. A small wooden bridge carries some of that motion into the body of the violin, which helps send sound into the room.

cards.title: How does a water meter know how much water a building used?
cards.summary: A water meter measures the amount of water passing along a pipe. When someone uses a sink or a shower, water can pass through the building’s meter on its way there.

cards.title: How does a web address tell a browser what to open?
cards.summary: A web address is often called a URL. It can name a site and say which thing you want there.

cards.title: How does a wood frog survive part of its body freezing?
cards.summary: A wood frog can spend the winter under leaves near the ground. As its surroundings get cold, some water outside its cells can turn to ice.

cards.title: How does a woodcut make a picture?
cards.summary: To make a woodcut, an artist carves away the parts of a flat block that should stay blank on the picture. The raised parts that are left get covered with ink.

cards.title: How does a zipper join two rows of teeth?
cards.summary: A zipper has two rows of shaped teeth and a part called a slider. When the slider moves one way, it guides the rows together so the teeth catch beside each other.

cards.title: How does American Sign Language work?
cards.summary: American Sign Language, or ASL, is a language that people can see. Signers use their hands, faces, and bodies to express ideas.

cards.title: How does an Asian elephant use its trunk?
cards.summary: An Asian elephant can pull a branch close, pick up a tiny object, and raise a load of water with the same tool: its trunk. A trunk is an extended nose and upper lip.

cards.title: How does an eastern chipmunk carry so many seeds?
cards.summary: A chipmunk has a cheek pouch on each side of its mouth that can stretch. The pouches hold several small seeds to the sides until it can put them down.

cards.title: How does an eastern cottontail stay close to cover?
cards.summary: An eastern cottontail often feeds on grass or low plants near a tangle of bushes. If something startles it, the rabbit can bolt into thick cover where a larger animal may have trouble following.

cards.title: How does an insulated bottle keep a drink warm or cold?
cards.summary: An insulated bottle often has two walls with very little air in the space between them. With so little air there, heat has a harder time moving through the gap.

cards.title: How does an interpreter help two people understand each other?
cards.summary: An interpreter helps people understand a conversation when they use different spoken or signed languages. The interpreter listens or watches closely and gives the message in another language.

cards.title: How does an octopus fit into a narrow hole?
cards.summary: A giant Pacific octopus has eight strong arms with suckers and a soft body. The hard beak in the center of its arms is one of the widest hard parts it must fit through an opening.

cards.title: How does an orangutan move in a forest?
cards.summary: Orangutans spend much of their lives above the ground in the forests of Borneo and Sumatra. Their long arms help them reach for branches, and their hands and feet can hold on from different angles.

cards.title: How does an osprey keep hold of a slippery fish?
cards.summary: An osprey can spot a fish near the surface while flying over water. It drops down and extends its feet to grab the fish.

cards.title: How does barter work?
cards.summary: Barter means trading something directly for something else. You might trade a comic you have already read for a book a friend has finished.

cards.title: How does Boolean logic use true and false?
cards.summary: Some computer questions have two possible answers. A door is open or it is not.

cards.title: How does borrowing money work?
cards.summary: A loan is money someone lends you under an agreement that you will pay it back. Imagine borrowing five dollars to buy art paper, knowing you can return the five next week.

cards.title: How does computer memory hold what you are using?
cards.summary: Think of your desk while you work. You may set out just the books and papers you need right now.

cards.title: How does cotton grow on a plant?
cards.summary: A cotton plant makes a dry fruit often called a boll. Inside that fruit, fine soft hairs grow from the surface of the seeds.

cards.title: How does erosion leave a narrow tower of stone?
cards.summary: A hoodoo is a tall, narrow shape made by rock wearing away unevenly. At Bryce Canyon, water enters cracks and can freeze when it gets cold.

cards.title: How does Hagia Sophia hold up its great dome?
cards.summary: Hagia Sophia is a historic building in Istanbul. Its builders had to fit a curved dome above a room with a square central space.

cards.title: How does insulation slow heat moving through a wall?
cards.summary: Heat tends to move from warmer places to cooler ones. Insulation inside a wall or roof makes that movement harder.

cards.title: How does liquid milk become solid cheese?
cards.summary: In many kinds of cheese making, a change in milk makes its proteins gather to form soft parts called curds. A watery liquid called whey can drain away.

cards.title: How does locking your device help protect it?
cards.summary: If you leave a tablet open, a person nearby may be able to read what you were doing or use an app that is already signed in. A device lock puts up a new check before letting someone get back to those things.

cards.title: How does moving your body help it work well?
cards.summary: When you move enough to breathe faster, your heart and lungs are moving more oxygen around your body. Over time, regular movement can help them do those jobs well.

cards.title: How does new seafloor form?
cards.summary: Long chains of underwater mountains rise along parts of the ocean floor. Many form where two plates move apart.

cards.title: How does one cell become two?
cards.summary: As you grow, the number of cells in your body goes up. One way it happens is that a cell copies its DNA and gets the two matching sets ready to move apart.

cards.title: How does regenerative braking save energy as a car slows?
cards.summary: Some electric and hybrid vehicles use their motor to help slow the wheels. The turning wheels drive the motor like a generator, which makes electricity from motion.

cards.title: How does soap help water wash away grease?
cards.summary: A greasy surface can make plain water form separate drops. Soap changes how these materials meet.

cards.title: How does soft clay become a hard bowl?
cards.summary: Potters can shape damp clay before it dries, when its small particles can move past one another. Drying takes out water and helps the shape hold.

cards.title: How does soft clay become a hard pot?
cards.summary: Wet clay can be pressed, rolled, or shaped as a wheel turns. A potter lets the finished shape dry before putting it into a special oven called a kiln.

cards.title: How does stainless steel resist rust?
cards.summary: Stainless steel has iron mixed with enough of a metal called chromium to make a very thin protective layer on its surface. That layer forms when chromium meets oxygen.

cards.title: How does stop-motion make objects look alive?
cards.summary: Set a toy on a table, take a picture, and move it a tiny bit. Take another picture and repeat.

cards.title: How does sunlight get into a food chain?
cards.summary: Green plants use energy from sunlight to make sugars from water and a gas in the air called carbon dioxide. A plant uses those sugars to grow.

cards.title: How does table tennis use the table in a rally?
cards.summary: A table tennis point starts when a player tosses a ball and strikes it so it bounces on their half of the table and then the other player’s half. After the serve, returns go directly toward the far side.

cards.title: How does tree sap become maple syrup?
cards.summary: In places with suitable weather, maple sap can flow well when nights are cold and days warm in late winter or spring. Sap from a sugar maple is usually clear and contains much more water than sugar.

cards.title: How does vitamin D help bones?
cards.summary: Vitamin D helps your gut take in calcium from food. Calcium is one of the materials your body uses to build strong bones and teeth.

cards.title: How does water reach the top of a tree?
cards.summary: When water leaves a tree’s leaves as vapor, it helps pull more water upward. Water molecules tend to cling to one another.

cards.title: How does weaving turn threads into cloth?
cards.summary: A weaver stretches one set of threads in order. Those threads are the warp.

cards.title: How does white clover creep across a lawn?
cards.summary: A stem of white clover can lie flat on top of the soil. As it grows longer, roots can form where parts of the stem touch the ground.

cards.title: How does Wi-Fi connect a device without a cable?
cards.summary: Wi-Fi is one way for a device to join a nearby network. Instead of a cable to the device, it uses radio signals.

cards.title: How does wind build a hill out of sand?
cards.summary: Wind can bounce small sand grains along the ground. If the wind slows near a plant, rock, or other obstacle, loose grains can pile up.

cards.title: How does witch hazel shoot some of its seeds away?
cards.summary: On common witch hazel, a ripe seed case can dry and bend out of shape. The squeezing sides can suddenly force a seed out, a little like a wet soap bar slipping from a tight hand.

cards.title: How does yeast make bread rise?
cards.summary: Bread yeast is a tiny living fungus. When it finds sugars available in dough, it can use them and release carbon dioxide gas.

cards.title: How does your blood plug a cut?
cards.summary: If a tiny vessel is damaged, its walls can squeeze inward to slow the flow. Small bits of cells called platelets stick to the broken spot and to each other.

cards.title: How does your body keep its balance?
cards.summary: Your brain checks several clues to see whether you are upright or tipping. Eyes can tell you how the room is moving in your view.

cards.title: How does your brain send messages?
cards.summary: Reaching for a pencil starts with messages traveling between nerve cells. A nerve cell is called a neuron.

cards.title: How does your brain talk to hormone glands?
cards.summary: A tiny gland under your brain is called the pituitary. A nearby part of your brain helps tell it what to release.

cards.title: How does your heart move blood?
cards.summary: Put a hand over your chest and you may feel your heart beating. Each beat is a squeeze from a muscle about the size of your fist.

cards.title: How does your rib cage protect you?
cards.summary: Your ribs curve around your chest like a long set of hoops. At the back they join the spine.

cards.title: How drinking water gets cleaned
cards.summary: Water from a river or lake can carry dirt and tiny living things. A treatment plant can add substances that help tiny bits of dirt clump together.

cards.title: How electric motors make things move
cards.summary: An electric motor makes a part turn. When electricity flows through a coil of wire, the wire makes a magnetic field.

cards.title: How electricity gets to your home
cards.summary: Power plants and other sources make electricity in many places. The power grid links these sources to towns, cities and buildings.

cards.title: How erosion carries rock and soil away
cards.summary: Erosion happens when water, wind, ice, or gravity moves soil and bits of rock. Rain can wash dirt from a path into a ditch.

cards.title: How escalator steps go flat at the top
cards.summary: An escalator runs a loop of steps around on a long chain. The visible steps ride upward or downward on wheels set in tracks.

cards.title: How far does sunlight reach into the ocean?
cards.summary: When you travel down through clear ocean water, the sunlight gets weaker. Near the top, enough light reaches plants and tiny algae for them to make food.

cards.title: How far is it around a circle?
cards.summary: Wrap a thread once around the outside of a flat round lid and measure the thread. That gives its circumference.

cards.title: How fiber optics guide a flash of light
cards.summary: A fiber-optic cable contains thin threads of glass or plastic. Light travels down a thread because its core and the layer around it bend light differently.

cards.title: How flowing water makes electricity
cards.summary: Water falling downhill can push blades around a wheel called a turbine. The turbine turns a generator, which sends electricity into wires.

cards.title: How gliders fly without an engine
cards.summary: A glider has wings but no engine to keep it moving forward. After a launch or a tow, the glider normally loses height as it moves through still air.

cards.title: How helicopters hover and turn
cards.summary: A helicopter’s main rotor spins long blades through the air. Each blade pushes air down and receives an upward push.

cards.title: How hurricanes get their strength
cards.summary: A hurricane is a large spinning storm that grows over warm ocean water. Warm, moist air rises from the sea.

cards.title: How Ingenuity flew in the thin air of Mars
cards.summary: The small helicopter Ingenuity rode to Mars under the Perseverance rover. The air on Mars is much thinner than on Earth, so there are fewer gas molecules for rotor blades to push against.

cards.title: How is a compound different from a mixture?
cards.summary: A compound forms when atoms of different elements join in a fixed pattern or proportion. Water is a compound.

cards.title: How is a sculpture different from a drawing?
cards.summary: A sculpture takes up space that you can measure in three directions: height, width, and depth. You might walk around a statue and see different details on each side.

cards.title: How is a sphere different from a circle?
cards.summary: A circle is flat, like the outline you draw around the bottom of a cup. A sphere is round in every direction, like a smooth ball.

cards.title: How large was a real Velociraptor?
cards.summary: Velociraptor was about as long as an adult human lying down, but much of that length was its tail. It was shorter and lighter than many movie raptors.

cards.title: How likely is something to happen?
cards.summary: Probability tells how likely an event is. A fair coin has two equally likely sides, so the chance it lands heads is one half.

cards.title: How lions live and hunt together
cards.summary: Lions often spend time in groups called prides. Females in a pride are often related, and they may care for cubs together.

cards.title: How liquid can push up a heavy machine
cards.summary: When you squeeze liquid in a closed set of tubes, the extra pressure is passed to other connected parts. A small push on a narrow piston makes a pressure change that is passed to a wide piston.

cards.title: How living things change over generations
cards.summary: Living things often have small differences from others of the same kind. Suppose some beetles have a color that makes it harder for birds to spot them.

cards.title: How magnets pull and push
cards.summary: A magnet can pull some materials toward it without touching them. Iron is one example.

cards.title: How many times did John Glenn circle Earth in Friendship 7?
cards.summary: In 1962, John Glenn rode a small spacecraft named Friendship 7 around Earth three times. He was the first American to go into orbit.

cards.title: How moving air and water carry heat
cards.summary: When a heater warms nearby air, that air often spreads out and becomes less dense. Cooler, denser air pushes it upward and moves into its place.

cards.title: How plants make their own food
cards.summary: A green plant uses sunlight, water, and a gas called carbon dioxide to make sugar. This is photosynthesis.

cards.title: How pollen travels from flower to flower
cards.summary: Flowers can make tiny grains called pollen. For many flowers to make seeds, pollen must reach a part of a flower that can receive it.

cards.title: How propellers push through air
cards.summary: Each blade of a spinning propeller acts like a small wing. Its slanted shape changes the pressure around it and pushes air backward.

cards.title: How quartz helps a clock count seconds
cards.summary: A quartz clock contains a little piece of a mineral that can vibrate. An electronic circuit gives the quartz small pushes so it vibrates at a regular rate.

cards.title: How railway signals help keep trains apart
cards.summary: One way to manage a railway is to divide it into sections called blocks. Equipment can tell a signaling system whether a train is in a block.

cards.title: How rainbows form
cards.summary: A rainbow can appear when sunlight shines into water drops in the air. The light bends on its way into a drop, bounces off the inside, and bends again as it leaves.

cards.title: How seeds start new plants
cards.summary: A seed holds the beginnings of a new plant. A coat helps protect the tiny plant inside.

cards.title: How ships use sound to map the seafloor
cards.summary: A ship can send a short sound into the water and wait for an echo from the bottom. Sound travels at a speed that researchers can estimate from the water’s conditions.

cards.title: How solar panels make electricity
cards.summary: A solar panel is made of smaller units called cells. When light reaches a cell, it can give energy to electrons inside the material.

cards.title: How sound moves through the air
cards.summary: Sound starts with something moving back and forth. When you pluck a guitar string, it shakes the air nearby.

cards.title: How spacecraft borrow speed from planets
cards.summary: Passing near a moving planet can change the path of a spacecraft. The planet’s gravity bends the spacecraft’s path as it flies past.

cards.title: How steam turned a locomotive’s wheels
cards.summary: A steam locomotive carries a boiler that heats water until it becomes steam. Pressure builds as the steam is kept inside.

cards.title: How submarines dive and rise
cards.summary: A submarine floats when water pushes upward as strongly as gravity pulls it downward. To dive, it lets seawater enter some tanks, replacing air.

cards.title: How sunlight warms Earth through empty space
cards.summary: The space between Earth and the Sun is mostly empty, so air cannot carry the Sun’s heat all the way here. Energy travels through space as radiation, including visible light and infrared light.

cards.title: How the northern and southern lights glow
cards.summary: An aurora can look like a glowing ribbon moving across a dark sky. Far above the ground, fast particles give energy to oxygen and nitrogen in Earth’s atmosphere.

cards.title: How the three main kinds of rock form
cards.summary: Scientists group rocks by the way they formed. Igneous rock forms when melted rock cools and hardens.

cards.title: How the Wright brothers learned to fly
cards.summary: Orville and Wilbur Wright tested gliders to learn how to balance an aircraft and turn it. They also made a wind tunnel to try different wing shapes before they built their powered Flyer.

cards.title: How tiny animals build coral reefs
cards.summary: A coral reef can look like a pile of rocks or plants, but it is built by small animals called coral polyps. Many kinds live in groups.

cards.title: How trains change tracks without steering
cards.summary: Train wheels follow metal rails, so a driver cannot turn a train the way a driver steers a car. At a junction, two short, tapered rails can move a little sideways.

cards.title: How was Ankylosaurus armored?
cards.summary: Ankylosaurus was a low, wide dinosaur that ate plants. Like the hard covering on a turtle, rows of bony plates helped protect it.

cards.title: How weather satellites watch moving storms
cards.summary: Weather satellites photograph Earth and measure kinds of light our eyes cannot see. A satellite high above the equator can go around once each day in the same direction as Earth turns.

cards.title: How wind turbines make electricity
cards.summary: A wind turbine turns moving air into electricity. When wind moves past the shaped blades, the difference in air pressure around them pushes them around.

cards.title: How wings hold up an airplane
cards.summary: A wing moving through air changes how the air moves over and under its surface. In flight, the wing pushes some air downward.

cards.title: Hungary
cards.summary: Most of Hungary is in a low basin surrounded by higher land in central Europe. The Danube divides Budapest, the capital, into parts that grew separately and are now connected by bridges.

cards.title: Iceland
cards.summary: Iceland is an island in the North Atlantic where very old ice and new volcanic rock can be found in the same country. Glaciers cover stretches of the interior, while heat close to the surface warms water underground.

cards.title: Idaho
cards.summary: Much of Idaho is mountain country, but a wide curve of lower land runs across the south. This is the Snake River Plain.

cards.title: Illinois
cards.summary: Illinois has water on several edges. Chicago stands on Lake Michigan in the northeast.

cards.title: India
cards.summary: India is a country in southern Asia. The Himalayas rise along its north, and a large part of the country reaches south into the Indian Ocean region.

cards.title: Indiana
cards.summary: Indiana touches Lake Michigan at its northwest corner, where sand dunes rise above the beach. The capital, Indianapolis, lies near the middle of the state, away from that lakeshore.

cards.title: Indonesia
cards.summary: Indonesia spreads along the equator on thousands of islands. Java contains Jakarta, one of the country’s largest cities and a major port.

cards.title: Io, Jupiter’s volcanic moon
cards.summary: Io is a moon of Jupiter with hundreds of volcanoes. Some send gas and dust high above its surface.

cards.title: Iowa
cards.summary: Iowa sits between two major rivers, the Mississippi on the east and the Missouri along much of its western edge. Much of the land between them is gently rolling and is used to grow crops.

cards.title: Ireland
cards.summary: Ireland can mean an island in the Atlantic or the country that covers most of it. The country’s capital, Dublin, is on the east coast.

cards.title: Is a horseshoe crab really a crab?
cards.summary: A horseshoe crab has a hard curved shell and a pointed tail. It belongs to a group more closely related to spiders than to true crabs.

cards.title: Is a narwhal’s tusk a horn?
cards.summary: A narwhal’s long spiral tusk is a tooth that grows out through its upper lip. The tusk is seen most often on males.

cards.title: Is a red clover head one big flower or many small ones?
cards.summary: A red clover's pink ball looks like one flower until you look closely. It is a flower head made of small flowers, each shaped a little like a pea flower.

cards.title: Is cement the same thing as concrete?
cards.summary: Cement is one ingredient in concrete. When you mix cement with water, it makes a paste.

cards.title: Is every square a rectangle?
cards.summary: To be a rectangle, a flat shape must have four straight sides and four right angles. A square has all of those things.

cards.title: Is ground fog really a cloud?
cards.summary: Fog is a cloud close enough to the ground for people to walk through it. On a quiet, clear night, the ground can lose heat.

cards.title: Is rhythm the same as the beat?
cards.summary: The beat is the steady pulse you can tap along to in much music. Rhythm is the pattern made by sounds and silences as time goes by.

cards.title: Is sea ice made from seawater?
cards.summary: Sea ice starts when ocean water becomes cold enough to freeze. Salt makes seawater freeze at a lower temperature than fresh water.

cards.title: Is the Web the same as the internet?
cards.summary: The Web is a huge collection of pages and other things that can get linked together. A browser gets a page from a place that can send it and lets you follow a link to another page.

cards.title: Italy
cards.summary: Italy reaches into the Mediterranean on a peninsula often compared with a boot. The Alps curve across the north, and the Apennine Mountains follow much of the length of the peninsula.

cards.title: Jamaica
cards.summary: Jamaica is an island in the Caribbean Sea south of Cuba. Its capital, Kingston, is on the southeast coast beside a large natural harbor.

cards.title: Japan
cards.summary: Japan is a chain of islands off the eastern side of Asia. A group of islands is called an archipelago.

cards.title: Jupiter, the biggest planet
cards.summary: Jupiter is the fifth planet from the Sun and the biggest in our solar system. It is about eleven times as wide as Earth.

cards.title: Kansas
cards.summary: The land rises gradually from eastern Kansas toward the west. Near Topeka, the capital, rivers wind through hilly areas.

cards.title: Kazakhstan
cards.summary: Kazakhstan is a very large inland country with grasslands stretching across much of the north and desert and dry hills farther south. High mountains rise toward the southeast.

cards.title: Kentucky
cards.summary: Kentucky has Appalachian hills in the east, gently rolling country around its middle and flatter river country in parts of the west. In the center, the Bluegrass region includes the state capital, Frankfort.

cards.title: Kenya
cards.summary: Kenya is in East Africa, and the equator runs across it. Its eastern coast meets the Indian Ocean.

cards.title: Kyrgyzstan
cards.summary: Mountains cover much of Kyrgyzstan, a landlocked country in Central Asia. Many belong to the Tian Shan range.

cards.title: Lake Baikal
cards.summary: Lake Baikal in Siberia is the deepest lake in the world. Looking at the thin shape it makes on a map gives little hint of how much water is below the surface.

cards.title: Laos
cards.summary: Laos is the only country in mainland Southeast Asia without a coast. Much of it is mountainous, but many settlements lie close to river valleys.

cards.title: Latvia
cards.summary: Latvia sits between Estonia and Lithuania on the eastern side of the Baltic Sea. Riga, the capital, stands near the mouth of the Daugava River on the Gulf of Riga.

cards.title: Lesotho
cards.summary: Lesotho is a country entirely surrounded by South Africa. It is unusually high: even the lowest places are more than a kilometer above sea level.

cards.title: Life aboard the International Space Station
cards.summary: The International Space Station is a science laboratory moving around Earth. Rockets carried its rooms and large pieces up one at a time.

cards.title: Life underground for naked mole-rats
cards.summary: A naked mole-rat lives in a network of tunnels beneath dry ground in eastern Africa. Its large front teeth stick out in front of its lips, so the animal can chew into dirt without filling its mouth with soil.

cards.title: Light and the colors we see
cards.summary: Light brings energy from one place to another. The Sun gives off light.

cards.title: Lithuania
cards.summary: Lithuania is the southernmost of the three Baltic states. Vilnius, the capital, is inland near the southeastern part of the country.

cards.title: Louisiana
cards.summary: The Mississippi River curves through southern Louisiana toward the Gulf. Its wide valley and low marshes look very different from the hills in parts of the north.

cards.title: Luxembourg
cards.summary: Luxembourg fits between Belgium, France, and Germany. The country and its capital city share the name Luxembourg.

cards.title: Madagascar
cards.summary: Madagascar is a large island off the southeast coast of Africa. Its high center contains Antananarivo, the capital.

cards.title: Maine
cards.summary: Maine is at the northeastern end of New England. Inland, forests cover a large part of the state and Mount Katahdin rises above nearby lakes and wooded valleys.

cards.title: Malawi
cards.summary: Malawi is a narrow inland country in southeastern Africa. Lake Malawi follows much of its eastern side, and some shores rise quickly into hills and higher land.

cards.title: Malaysia
cards.summary: Malaysia has two main parts with a sea between them. One sits at the southern end of the Malay Peninsula, where Kuala Lumpur is the capital.

cards.title: Maldives
cards.summary: The Maldives are small, low islands in the Indian Ocean southwest of India and Sri Lanka. Many are part of rings of coral and sand around shallow water called atolls.

cards.title: Mali
cards.summary: Mali is a large inland country in western Africa with a desert north and generally wetter land toward the south. Bamako, the capital, stands beside the Niger River.

cards.title: Malta
cards.summary: Malta is a small country made up of islands in the Mediterranean Sea, south of Sicily. The two largest islands are Malta and Gozo.

cards.title: Mars, the red planet
cards.summary: Mars looks red from far away because its dust and rocks contain a kind of iron that has rusted. Up close, the ground can also look brown, tan, or gold.

cards.title: Maryland
cards.summary: The Chesapeake Bay almost splits Maryland into separate pieces on a map. The Eastern Shore lies between the bay and the Atlantic coast.

cards.title: Massachusetts
cards.summary: Massachusetts has an Atlantic coast in the east and rolling hills and mountains in the west. Boston, the capital, grew around a harbor.

cards.title: Mercury, the closest planet to the Sun
cards.summary: Mercury is the smallest planet in our solar system and the closest one to the Sun. Its rocky ground is covered in round dents called craters.

cards.title: Mexico
cards.summary: Mexico is in North America, just south of the United States. The Pacific Ocean is on one side and the Gulf of Mexico is on the other.

cards.title: Michigan
cards.summary: Michigan has two big sections of land, called the Upper and Lower peninsulas. The Lower Peninsula is famous for looking a little like a mitten on a map.

cards.title: Minnesota
cards.summary: Minnesota has forests and many lakes in the north, more farmland toward the south and west, and a part of Lake Superior on its northeastern edge. The Mississippi River begins at Lake Itasca and winds across the state before turning south.

cards.title: Miranda’s cliffs and grooves
cards.summary: Miranda is one of the larger moons of Uranus, though it measures less than 500 kilometers across. Some parts of it have lots of round craters.

cards.title: Mississippi
cards.summary: Mississippi reaches from the lower Mississippi River valley to the Gulf Coast. The western side includes low, flat land by the river.

cards.title: Missouri
cards.summary: The Missouri River crosses the state from west to east and joins the Mississippi near St. Louis.

cards.title: Mongolia
cards.summary: Mongolia sits in inland Asia between Russia and China. The Gobi Desert takes up part of the south, while wide grasslands spread across much of the country.

cards.title: Montana
cards.summary: Montana has steep mountains in its west and broad, more open plains toward its east. Helena, the state capital, sits in the western part of the state.

cards.title: Morocco
cards.summary: Morocco is in northwestern Africa. The Atlantic Ocean meets the country on the west, and the Mediterranean meets it on the north.

cards.title: Mount Kilimanjaro
cards.summary: Mount Kilimanjaro rises from the plains of northern Tanzania to the highest point in Africa. It is made of several volcanoes joined together.

cards.title: Mozambique
cards.summary: Mozambique has a long coast on the Indian Ocean. The Zambezi River reaches the coast across the middle of the country, carrying water from far inland.

cards.title: Myanmar
cards.summary: Myanmar, also called Burma, runs from high mountains in the north to the coast of the Indian Ocean. The Ayeyarwady River flows south through much of the country, passing wide farming areas and spreading into a delta near the coast.

cards.title: Namibia
cards.summary: Namibia lies on the Atlantic coast of southwestern Africa. Near the sea, the Namib Desert contains stretches of gravel and huge sand dunes.

cards.title: Nebraska
cards.summary: Nebraska stretches west from the Missouri River into the Great Plains. Lincoln, its capital, is near the eastern end.

cards.title: Nepal
cards.summary: Nepal follows the southern slopes of the Himalayas between India and China. Along its southern side the ground is much lower and flatter.

cards.title: Neptune, the farthest planet
cards.summary: Neptune is the eighth planet from the Sun, so a trip around the Sun takes about 165 Earth years. It is cold at the tops of its clouds, and powerful winds sweep across them.

cards.title: Netherlands
cards.summary: The Netherlands lies on the North Sea, where several European rivers reach the coast. Much of the ground is low and flat.

cards.title: Nevada
cards.summary: Nevada has many mountain ranges with long, lower valleys between them. Much of the state is in the Great Basin, where rain and snowmelt collect inland instead of flowing to the sea.

cards.title: New Hampshire
cards.summary: New Hampshire includes high mountains, lake country, wooded river valleys and a short Atlantic coast. The White Mountains lie well north of the capital, Concord, and include Mount Washington.

cards.title: New Jersey
cards.summary: New Jersey lies between the Delaware River and the Atlantic Ocean. Trenton, the capital, is on the river across from Pennsylvania.

cards.title: New Mexico
cards.summary: New Mexico stretches from mountains in the north to dry plains and valleys farther south. Santa Fe, the state capital, sits high above sea level in the northern part of the state.

cards.title: New York
cards.summary: New York City sits at the southern end of the state, where the Hudson River reaches tidal waters and a busy harbor. Far upriver, Albany is the state capital.

cards.title: New Zealand
cards.summary: New Zealand lies in the southwestern Pacific Ocean and includes two main islands. A narrow passage called Cook Strait separates them.

cards.title: Nicaragua
cards.summary: Nicaragua’s west side has volcanoes and two large lakes close to the Pacific coast. Managua, the capital, is beside the smaller Lake Managua.

cards.title: Niger
cards.summary: Niger is a landlocked country in western Africa immediately north of Nigeria. A large share of its land lies in the Sahara, and dry country stretches far across the map.

cards.title: Nigeria
cards.summary: Nigeria reaches inland from the Gulf of Guinea in western Africa. The Niger and Benue rivers meet near the center, then flow south to a broad delta.

cards.title: Nile River
cards.summary: The Nile flows north through northeastern Africa to the Mediterranean. The Blue Nile carries water from Ethiopia, and the White Nile brings water from areas farther south.

cards.title: North Carolina
cards.summary: North Carolina runs from the mountains in the west to the Atlantic in the east. Between them are rolling hills where Raleigh, the capital, is located.

cards.title: North Dakota
cards.summary: North Dakota lies in the northern Great Plains. The Missouri River flows past Bismarck, the state capital.

cards.title: North Korea
cards.summary: North Korea occupies the northern part of the Korean Peninsula. Much of its land is hilly or mountainous, and broad lowlands are more common toward the west.

cards.title: Norway
cards.summary: Norway is a long, narrow country on the west side of the Scandinavian Peninsula. In many places the sea reaches inland between high rocky slopes.

cards.title: Ohio
cards.summary: Ohio has a Great Lake on one side and a large river on another. To the north, cities such as Cleveland grew beside Lake Erie.

cards.title: Oklahoma
cards.summary: Oklahoma spreads from flatter, drier land in the west to hills and forests toward its east. A long strip called the Panhandle reaches out at the northwest.

cards.title: Oregon
cards.summary: Oregon’s Pacific coast has cliffs, beaches and forested headlands. Inland from the coast are valleys, including the Willamette Valley where Salem, the capital, is located.

cards.title: Our solar system
cards.summary: The solar system is our Sun and everything held in orbit by its gravity. That includes eight planets, their moons, dwarf planets, and smaller objects such as asteroids and comets.

cards.title: Pakistan
cards.summary: Pakistan stretches from some of the world’s highest mountains in the north to the Arabian Sea in the south. The Indus River runs down through the country and brings water to many fields.

cards.title: Panama
cards.summary: Panama is a narrow country between the Caribbean Sea and the Pacific Ocean. Its shape makes it part of the land bridge connecting Central and South America.

cards.title: Paraguay
cards.summary: The Paraguay River runs down through the country that shares its name. To the west lies part of the Gran Chaco, a broad landscape where many places are dry and hot.

cards.title: Pennsylvania
cards.summary: Pennsylvania’s middle has long ridges with valleys between them, part of the Appalachian region. Harrisburg, the capital, stands on the Susquehanna River in that part of the state.

cards.title: Perseverance, a robot geologist on Mars
cards.summary: Perseverance is a car-sized robot that landed in Jezero Crater in 2021. That place has a fan of rock left where a river once carried material into a lake.

cards.title: Peru
cards.summary: Peru runs along the Pacific coast of South America. Lima, the capital, is along the dry coastal strip.

cards.title: Philippines
cards.summary: The Philippines is a large group of islands in the western Pacific Ocean. Many maps group the islands into Luzon in the north, the Visayas in the middle, and Mindanao in the south.

cards.title: Phobos and Deimos, the moons of Mars
