cards.title: What makes a place a freshwater wetland?
cards.summary: A freshwater wetland has water in or above the soil for long enough to shape which plants and animals can live there. Some wetlands have puddles you can see.

cards.title: What makes a place a World Heritage Site?
cards.summary: Some places hold clues about Earth or human history that people across the world can learn from. Countries can propose special places for an international list kept through UNESCO.

cards.title: What makes a plant native to a place?
cards.summary: A plant is native to a region when it occurs there naturally rather than arriving because people brought it from somewhere else. A plant native to one part of a country might not be native to another part.

cards.title: What makes a plateau different from a mountain peak?
cards.summary: A plateau is a high area of land with a broad, fairly level top. A single sharp mountain peak comes to a much smaller point.

cards.title: What makes a purple passionflower look like a clock face?
cards.summary: A purple passionflower can look as if somebody placed a ring of thin threads on top of a wide flower. The threads spread out from the middle over the outer parts, making rings of purple and white.

cards.title: What makes a Queen Anne's lace flower head look like lace?
cards.summary: A head of Queen Anne's lace can look flat from the side and lacy when you look down at it. Many little white flowers sit on groups of stalks that spread like the ribs of an umbrella.

cards.title: What makes a shagbark hickory look scruffy?
cards.summary: Look at an older shagbark hickory trunk and you may see thick strips of gray outer bark peeling away from it. The ends of the strips often stick out, while parts of the strips remain attached.

cards.title: What makes a snare drum buzz when you play it?
cards.summary: A snare drum has a stretched head on top and another thin head underneath. A tap sets the top head moving and can make the lower one move too.

cards.title: What makes a star explode as a supernova?
cards.summary: A supernova is an explosion that can make a star suddenly extremely bright. One kind happens when a very massive star’s center collapses and a blast sends much of the rest of the star outward.

cards.title: What makes a tradition living heritage?
cards.summary: Living heritage includes things people learn from others and still practice, like telling stories, playing a style of music, or making baskets in a special way. A museum can save a basket, but the skill of making that kind of basket stays alive when people keep doing it and teach it.

cards.title: What makes a tsunami different from wind waves?
cards.summary: A tsunami starts when a great amount of ocean water is suddenly pushed out of place. An earthquake that lifts or drops part of the ocean floor can start one.

cards.title: What makes an angle wide or narrow?
cards.summary: An angle shows how far one direction turns from another. Open a book a little.

cards.title: What makes an ecosystem
cards.summary: An ecosystem includes living things in a place, the parts of the place that are not alive, and the ways they affect one another. Think of a pond.

cards.title: What makes an old-growth forest special?
cards.summary: An old-growth forest has had a long time to develop features that are often missing from younger forests. There may be very large old trees, smaller young ones, and trunks lying on the ground.

cards.title: What makes fruit jam thick enough to spread?
cards.summary: A lot of fruits contain a substance called pectin. Under the right conditions, pectin molecules form a loose network that can hold water.

cards.title: What makes hook-and-loop fasteners stick together?
cards.summary: One side of a hook-and-loop fastener has many tiny hooks. The soft side has small loops.

cards.title: What makes ice cream feel smooth instead of icy?
cards.summary: As ice cream freezes, some of its water forms solid ice crystals. A mixture with many tiny crystals can feel smooth on your tongue.

cards.title: What makes lightning and thunder
cards.summary: Inside a storm cloud, bits of ice can bump into each other and help separate electric charges. As the charges build up, electricity can suddenly move through the air.

cards.title: What makes little bumps rise on your skin?
cards.summary: You might see rows of little bumps on your arm in the cold, or while listening to exciting music. Each bump can happen when a tiny muscle tugs at a hair near its base.

cards.title: What makes long holes in a tree trunk?
cards.summary: A pileated woodpecker uses its strong bill to chip pieces of wood away. It may leave a long, roughly rectangular hole while it searches for carpenter ants and other insects in a trunk or log.

cards.title: What makes ocean currents flow
cards.summary: An ocean current is water moving from one place to another. In shallow areas near the coast, the tide can make water flow into a bay and later flow out.

cards.title: What makes Old Faithful famous?
cards.summary: Old Faithful is a geyser in Yellowstone National Park. Water under the ground gets very hot, and steam and water rush out when enough pressure builds.

cards.title: What makes some twins identical?
cards.summary: Identical twins come from one fertilized egg that begins developing and divides into two groups of cells. This gives them almost the same DNA from the beginning.

cards.title: What makes something a chemical element
cards.summary: A chemical element is a kind of substance made of atoms that all have the same number of protons. Every gold atom has 79 protons, so a very pure piece of gold has atoms of just one element.

cards.title: What makes something a mixture?
cards.summary: A bowl with rice and beans holds a mixture. You can add more of either food and still recognize the pieces.

cards.title: What makes something a primary source?
cards.summary: A primary source is direct evidence about the question you are studying. If you want to learn what a person saw at a parade, their own letter about it can be a primary source.

cards.title: What makes something a secondary source?
cards.summary: A secondary source explains or interprets information somebody else recorded, saw, or made. For a project about the history of a park, a new book based on old maps, letters, and interviews can be a secondary source.

cards.title: What makes the design of Angkor Wat unusual?
cards.summary: Angkor Wat is a large Khmer temple in Cambodia. A wide water-filled moat surrounds its grounds.

cards.title: What makes the first vibration inside a saxophone?
cards.summary: A saxophone player blows air through a small gap next to a thin strip called a reed. The reed bends and springs back many times each second, changing the flow of air into the instrument.

cards.title: What makes the Ozarks hillier than nearby plains?
cards.summary: The Ozarks spread across parts of Missouri, Arkansas, Oklahoma and nearby Kansas. In much of the region, the land is high enough for streams to cut downward and leave steep valleys between the hills.

cards.title: What makes the wind blow?
cards.summary: Air pushes on things even when it looks empty. When air pushes more strongly in one place than in a nearby place, it starts moving from the higher pressure toward lower pressure.

cards.title: What makes two halves match?
cards.summary: Draw a heart, then imagine folding it down the middle. If every part of one half lands on the same part of the other half, the fold is a line of symmetry.

cards.title: What minerals are
cards.summary: A mineral is a solid that forms in nature and has a certain kind of material and pattern inside it. Quartz is one mineral.

cards.title: What part of a flax plant becomes linen?
cards.summary: A flax plant grows long groups of tough fibers inside its slender stems. After harvest, people loosen and remove other stem material so they can gather those fibers.

cards.title: What part of a fungus is a mushroom?
cards.summary: A mushroom can be the visible part of a fungus that makes and releases spores. Much of the same fungus may be growing as fine threads in soil, leaves or wood.

cards.title: What path did Pioneer 10 take to reach Jupiter?
cards.summary: Pioneer 10 left Earth in 1972 and became the first spacecraft to pass through the main asteroid belt. It then flew by Jupiter and sent back close measurements of the great planet and its surroundings.

cards.title: What protects the outside of a tooth?
cards.summary: The part of a tooth that sticks above your gums wears a hard coat called enamel. It is tough enough to protect the tooth through lots of biting and chewing.

cards.title: What remains when a Sun-like star sheds its outer layers?
cards.summary: When a star close to the Sun’s size reaches its final stages, it can send its outer layers drifting away. The very dense center left behind is called a white dwarf.

cards.title: What rule means one or the other, but never both?
cards.summary: An imaginary sign might light up when only one person presses a button. If neither presses a button, it stays dark.

cards.title: What shape is a ginkgo leaf?
cards.summary: A ginkgo leaf spreads out like a little fan on a long handle. Lines of tiny tubes start near the handle and fork again and again as they reach the wide edge.

cards.title: What shaped the Sierra Nevada mountains?
cards.summary: The Sierra Nevada is a long mountain range mainly in eastern California, along the western side of Nevada. Large bodies of rock, including granite, make up many of its high slopes.

cards.title: What shaped Yosemite Valley?
cards.summary: Yosemite Valley in California has huge granite cliffs, including El Capitan. Granite is a hard rock that formed when melted rock cooled deep underground.

cards.title: What shapes make the Sydney Opera House easy to recognize?
cards.summary: The Sydney Opera House stands beside the harbor in Sydney, Australia. Its light-colored roofs look like pieces of shells, and some people think they look like sails.

cards.title: What should you notice before sharing a photo?
cards.summary: A picture may show more than you meant to share. Look at the background.

cards.title: What shows that Norse travelers reached North America?
cards.summary: At L’Anse aux Meadows on Newfoundland, archaeologists found traces of buildings and objects made by Norse travelers. Turf once covered parts of the structures, helping people live in a windy coastal place.

cards.title: What sticks out between the scales of a Douglas-fir cone?
cards.summary: A Douglas-fir cone has thin parts sticking out between its overlapping scales. Each of these parts has three points.

cards.title: What surprising clue did Explorer 1 find above Earth?
cards.summary: Explorer 1 was the first U.S. satellite, launched in January 1958.

cards.title: What tells a musician how fast to play?
cards.summary: Tempo is the speed of the beat in music. Imagine walking with a steady drum tap.

cards.title: What turns inside a crank pencil sharpener?
cards.summary: A crank pencil sharpener has small cutters inside that roll around the tip of the pencil when you turn the handle. The cutters shave away thin pieces of wood and shape the dark part in the middle into a point.

cards.title: What voting rule did the Fifteenth Amendment add?
cards.summary: The Fifteenth Amendment says the United States and states cannot deny or reduce voting rights on account of race, color, or having been enslaved. States approved it in 1870.

cards.title: What was a trilobite?
cards.summary: A trilobite was a small ocean animal related to today’s insects, spiders, and crabs. Its outer shell was divided along its length into a center section and two side sections.

cards.title: What was ancient Greece?
cards.summary: Ancient Greece included many communities around the sea. Some cities and the area around each city formed a separate government.

cards.title: What was apartheid in South Africa?
cards.summary: Apartheid was a system of laws in South Africa that separated people by race. It gave white people most political power and put limits on where many other people could live, travel, study, or work.

cards.title: What was it like to live and work in Skylab?
cards.summary: Skylab was the first U.S. space station.

cards.title: What was Persepolis built to show?
cards.summary: Persepolis was a royal center in ancient Persia. Its builders made a huge level platform along a mountainside.

cards.title: What was the city at Cahokia Mounds like?
cards.summary: Cahokia was a large Indigenous city near the Mississippi River, in what is now Illinois. Its people carried loads of soil to make raised mounds.

cards.title: What was the city of Ur?
cards.summary: Ur was a large city in southern Mesopotamia. One of its best-known buildings was a ziggurat with stepped levels that rose above the flat ground.

cards.title: What was the Kingdom of Kush?
cards.summary: Kush was a kingdom farther up the Nile from Egypt, in what is now Sudan. People there built towns, temples, and burial places.

cards.title: What was the Louisiana Purchase?
cards.summary: In 1803, the United States bought France’s claim to a large stretch of land west of the Mississippi River. American leaders wanted a reliable place to send goods through New Orleans, a busy port near the river’s mouth.

cards.title: What was the thick dome on Pachycephalosaurus?
cards.summary: Pachycephalosaurus walked on two legs and had an unusually thick dome of bone on top of its skull. Smaller bony bumps surrounded part of the head.

cards.title: What was the Underground Railroad?
cards.summary: The Underground Railroad was a loose network of people, routes, and hiding places that helped enslaved people seeking freedom. Some people left on their own and received help along the way.

cards.title: What were Indus seals?
cards.summary: Archaeologists have found small carved seals at ancient Indus sites. A seal has a design that can be pressed into soft material, leaving a mark.

cards.title: What were oracle bones used for?
cards.summary: During the Shang dynasty, people at the royal court asked questions about what might happen. A question could be about rain, crops, or a trip.

cards.title: What were the three horns of Triceratops for?
cards.summary: Triceratops walked on four legs and ate plants. Two long horns rose above its eyes, and it had a smaller horn over its nose.

cards.title: What’s the difference between melody and harmony?
cards.summary: The melody is the line of notes you might hum when you remember a song. Harmony comes from notes sounding together or from the way groups of notes change underneath that tune.

cards.title: When are two shapes exactly the same size and shape?
cards.summary: Two shapes are congruent if you can make one fit exactly over the other by moving it, turning it or flipping it. Cut two triangles from the same cardboard pattern.

cards.title: When can you group numbers in a different way?
cards.summary: When you add three numbers, you can choose which pair to add first while keeping the numbers in the same order. For five plus eight plus two, you might add eight and two first because they make ten.

cards.title: When can you swap numbers without changing the answer?
cards.summary: You can swap the order of two numbers when adding or multiplying them and still get the same answer. Three groups of five tiles and five groups of three tiles both make 15 tiles.

cards.title: When does a new plant or animal become invasive?
cards.summary: Some living things reach new places when people carry boats, plants, soil, or other goods between regions. Some newcomers never establish a wild population.

cards.title: When does an AND rule say yes?
cards.summary: Imagine a pretend treasure chest that opens only when you have a key and stand on a marked square. You need both parts.

cards.title: When does an OR rule say yes?
cards.summary: Suppose a pretend gate opens if you have a round token or a square token. With either token the gate opens.

cards.title: When is a piece of land called a peninsula?
cards.summary: A peninsula sticks out into water but stays joined to a larger piece of land. Most of Florida reaches out between the Atlantic Ocean and the Gulf of Mexico, and a road can take you there without crossing either sea.

cards.title: Where an echo comes from
cards.summary: An echo is a sound you hear after it bounces off a surface and returns. At the edge of a canyon, a shout can travel to a cliff and back.

cards.title: Where are we in the Milky Way?
cards.summary: The Sun is one star in a huge disk of stars called the Milky Way. If you could look down on that disk from well above it, you would see a long bar of stars in the middle and spiral arms curving around it.

cards.title: Where can an old computer or phone go after someone stops using it?
cards.summary: A device that still works may be repaired or passed along for someone else to use. A device that is no longer useful can lose its job as a phone or computer while still containing materials worth keeping.

cards.title: Where did corn come from?
cards.summary: Corn, also called maize, grew into a farm crop from a wild plant called teosinte. This change began thousands of years ago in what is now Mexico.

cards.title: Where did the Winnie-the-Pooh characters come from?
cards.summary: English writer A. A.

cards.title: Where did Zheng He’s fleets travel?
cards.summary: In the early 1400s, the rulers of Ming China sent fleets of ships across the Indian Ocean. A leader named Zheng He commanded several of these journeys.

cards.title: Where do gutters take rain that lands on a roof?
cards.summary: Rain hitting a roof can run toward its lower edge. A gutter is a channel that catches some of the water there.

cards.title: Where do shore crabs hide when the tide goes out?
cards.summary: A shore crab on a rocky coast may duck into a narrow crack or shelter beneath a rock as the water drops away. These spots can stay cool and damp while open rock dries in the sun.

cards.title: Where do the Appalachian Mountains run?
cards.summary: The Appalachian Mountains form a long, old group of mountain ranges in eastern North America. Their ridges, valleys and high plateaus reach from eastern Canada into the southern United States.

cards.title: Where do the blue chicory flowers go in the afternoon?
cards.summary: You can see bright blue chicory flowers on some roadsides in the morning. A flower head may close later in the day, so the same plant can look much plainer in the afternoon.

cards.title: Where do the lines in a leaf go?
cards.summary: A leaf can look like a tiny road map if you hold it where light shines through. The big lines are veins, with finer lines leading away from them.

cards.title: Where do the materials in fallen leaves go?
cards.summary: A tree drops a leaf into the leaf litter on the ground. Small animals can tear it into pieces.

cards.title: Where does a battery get its energy?
cards.summary: A battery contains materials that can react with each other. You can connect the two ends into a circuit so the reaction helps move electrons around the outside path.

cards.title: Where does a dragonfly live before it can fly?
cards.summary: A young dragonfly lives underwater. In this stage it is called an aquatic nymph.

cards.title: Where does a fraction go on a number line?
cards.summary: To place three fourths on a number line, divide the space from zero to one into four equal steps. Start at zero and move three of those steps to the right.

cards.title: Where does a groundhog spend the winter?
cards.summary: A groundhog, also called a woodchuck, spends the coldest part of the year inside a burrow. It goes into hibernation, when its body cools and its heartbeat and breathing slow down.

cards.title: Where does a wild turkey sleep at night?
cards.summary: A wild turkey can spend much of a day walking on the ground. It may scratch through old leaves to find nuts, seeds, or insects.

cards.title: Where does dirt go inside a vacuum cleaner?
cards.summary: A vacuum cleaner uses a fast fan to move air from the hose or floor head toward an outlet. Air in the room rushes into the opening and carries loose dirt with it.

cards.title: Where does food go after you swallow it?
cards.summary: Digestion begins before you swallow. Your teeth break up food, and saliva starts breaking down some of it.

cards.title: Where does hair grow from?
cards.summary: A hair gets longer from the end hidden inside the skin. That end sits in a small pocket called a follicle.

cards.title: Where does rain on a street go?
cards.summary: After rain falls on a street, much of it cannot soak through the hard surface. Water runs along slopes and gutters to an opening or grate.

cards.title: Where does sugar go when it dissolves?
cards.summary: When sugar dissolves, it is still there even after you stop seeing the grains. Water separates the sugar molecules from the grain and surrounds them without breaking apart the individual molecules.

cards.title: Where does the Mississippi River begin and end?
cards.summary: The Mississippi River begins where water flows out of Lake Itasca in northern Minnesota. It is small at first, but it gathers water from many other streams and rivers on its way south.

cards.title: Where does the question mark go in Armenian?
cards.summary: An Armenian question mark is a small curved sign put above a vowel in the word that carries the question. It can point out which word asks for an answer.

cards.title: Where does the Rio Grande go after leaving the mountains?
cards.summary: The Rio Grande begins in the Rocky Mountains of southern Colorado. It flows into New Mexico, passing places such as Albuquerque.

cards.title: Where does vanilla flavor come from?
cards.summary: Vanilla can come from the fruit of a climbing orchid. People often call the long fruit a vanilla bean, even though it is an orchid pod.

cards.title: Where does water go on the two sides of the Rocky Mountain divide?
cards.summary: In Rocky Mountain National Park, the high ridge known as the Continental Divide sends rain and melted snow along very different routes. Streams on the west side of the ridge feed the Colorado River.

cards.title: Where is Hawaii’s hidden undersea volcano?
cards.summary: South of the Big Island of Hawaiʻi, an active volcano called Kamaʻehuakanaloa rises from the bottom of the Pacific. Its top is still far below the water.

cards.title: Where is most of a fungus hiding?
cards.summary: A fungus often grows as a net of tiny branching threads. The whole net is called mycelium.

cards.title: Where is the deepest part of the ocean?
cards.summary: The ocean floor is not flat. Long, narrow valleys called trenches cut deeply below nearby areas.

cards.title: Where is the equator?
cards.summary: The equator is an imaginary circle around Earth halfway between the North Pole and the South Pole. It divides Earth into the Northern Hemisphere and Southern Hemisphere.

cards.title: Where is the intertidal zone?
cards.summary: Stand back from a shore and imagine two lines across it. One marks how high the water reaches at high tide.

cards.title: Where on a pumpkin vine does a pumpkin begin?
cards.summary: A pumpkin vine sends its stems across the ground. It can make flowers that release pollen and other flowers where fruits can start.

cards.title: Where very long-traveling comets may come from
cards.summary: Some comets pass the Sun once and may take thousands of years to return. Scientists think many begin in a vast outer region called the Oort Cloud.

cards.title: Where water goes after it runs down the drain
cards.summary: Water that leaves sinks or toilets can move through sewer pipes to a treatment plant. Screens catch big pieces of trash first.

cards.title: Which cave formations hang down and which grow up?
cards.summary: Water can pass through rock and carry dissolved material into a cave. As a drop hangs from the ceiling, it may leave a little solid mineral.

cards.title: Which lakes make up the Great Lakes?
cards.summary: Superior, Michigan, Huron, Erie, and Ontario are the five Great Lakes in North America. They are huge bodies of fresh water, and water moves between them through connected rivers and waterways.

cards.title: Which little spring flower looks like upside-down pants?
cards.summary: A row of white Dutchman's breeches flowers may look like tiny pants hung by their waists. Two pointed parts stick upward from each hanging flower.

cards.title: Which northern tree drops whole bunches of soft needles?
cards.summary: For part of summer, a tamarack twig carries lots of soft needles in little bunches. If you look at a new shoot, you can also see single needles along it.

cards.title: Which orange wildflower is also a milkweed?
cards.summary: A patch of butterfly weed can look like little orange umbrellas standing over the grass. Each umbrella is a cluster of small flowers.

cards.title: Which part of a calculation comes first?
cards.summary: If you see 2 + 3 × 4, you might think to add first. In the usual order of operations, multiplication comes before addition, so three times four is twelve and the total is fourteen.

cards.title: Which part of a carrot plant do we eat?
cards.summary: The familiar part of a carrot is a thick main root. It can hold food the plant made earlier in its green leaves.

cards.title: Which part of the Appalachians is called the Blue Ridge?
cards.summary: The Blue Ridge is one part of the longer Appalachian system in the eastern United States. Its mountains run across states including Virginia and North Carolina, and reach into nearby states.

cards.title: Which pieces of space rock reach the ground?
cards.summary: Many bits of space rock heat up during their fast trip into Earth’s air. They can make a streak of light called a meteor.

cards.title: Which pine grows in old fields in the southeastern U.S.?
cards.summary: A loblolly pine can grow in sunny places where farm fields or other open ground used to be. Seeds from nearby trees can find enough light there to start new trees.

cards.title: Which services can a town provide together?
cards.summary: People in a town share some services, such as roads, parks, and fire protection. A local government can organize those services for many people at once instead of each household trying to provide its own.

cards.title: Which shapes can tile a floor without leaving gaps?
cards.summary: A tessellation covers a flat surface with shapes that fit just up to one another, without gaps or overlaps. Squares can do it because four square corners meet exactly around one point.

cards.title: Which six states make up New England?
cards.summary: New England is a region in the far northeastern United States. It includes Connecticut, Maine, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, Rhode Island and Vermont.

cards.title: Which wetland plant can have a flower as wide as a dinner plate?
cards.summary: A swamp rose mallow can have flowers several inches across. The petals may be pale with a dark red center, or pink with darker marks.

cards.title: Who are producers and consumers?
cards.summary: A producer makes a good or supplies a service. A person who uses a good or service is a consumer.

cards.title: Who built the large palaces of ancient Crete?
cards.summary: The people we call Minoans lived on Crete thousands of years ago. They built large groups of rooms around open courts at places such as Knossos.

cards.title: Who carved the big stone figures on Rapa Nui?
cards.summary: Rapa Nui is a Chilean island far out in the Pacific Ocean. Its Indigenous Rapa Nui people carved large stone figures known as moai.

cards.title: Who checks whether the things a factory makes are right?
cards.summary: A quality control inspector checks parts or finished products against a plan. One piece may need to be a certain length.

cards.title: Who decides how products should get from one place to another?
cards.summary: People who work in logistics make plans for moving and storing things. If a shop needs boxes by Friday, someone has to find out where the boxes are, how much space they take, and which trip can get them there.

cards.title: Who designs the outdoor parts of a park?
cards.summary: A landscape architect plans outdoor places such as parks, plazas, and schoolyards. The job can include deciding where paths go, which parts stay open for play, and where trees can give shade.

cards.title: Who frees a fossil stuck inside a rock?
cards.summary: A fossil found outdoors may come to a museum with rock still stuck around it. A specialist called a fossil preparator studies where the fossil meets that rock.

cards.title: Who helps keep a grocery store’s shelves filled?
cards.summary: A grocery stock worker moves products from storage to the places where shoppers look for them. When several boxes look alike, the worker needs to check which exact product belongs in each space.

cards.title: Who helps keep an airplane’s equipment working?
cards.summary: Aircraft mechanics inspect, maintain, and repair equipment used on aircraft. An airplane depends on many parts working together, so checks include written instructions and records of what was done.

cards.title: Who keeps the grounds around a park or school ready to use?
cards.summary: Groundskeepers care for outdoor places people use. Their tasks depend on the place.

cards.title: Who lives in a dead tree that is still standing?
cards.summary: A dead tree that has not fallen is called a forest snag. As some of its wood softens, a woodpecker may dig a hole to nest in.

cards.title: Who lives in the seaweed washed onto a beach?
cards.summary: Waves often leave strips of seaweed and other natural material along a beach. This pile, called beach wrack, is food and shelter for small animals such as beach hoppers.

cards.title: Who looks after elevators and escalators?
cards.summary: Elevator and escalator technicians install or care for machines that move people between levels. In a new building they fit equipment into the planned space.

cards.title: Who looks after the wires that carry power through a town?
cards.summary: Power line workers install and repair the cables that bring electricity from the grid toward buildings. Some lines pass above streets, while other lines run underground.

cards.title: Who organizes games and activities at a recreation center?
cards.summary: A recreation worker helps people use their free time for things such as games, crafts, and sports. Planning might include choosing an activity, collecting materials, and deciding how to share a room among groups.

cards.title: Who puts the glass into a building?
cards.summary: A worker called a glazier fits glass into openings and fixtures. Glaziers might put in a shop window, a glass door, or a window in a roof.

cards.title: Who rode Vostok 1 around Earth?
cards.summary: In April 1961, Yuri Gagarin became the first human to travel into space. He rode in a round cabin on a Soviet spacecraft called Vostok 1.

cards.title: Who tells a story?
cards.summary: The narrator is the voice that tells the story. A storyteller who says “I opened the door” can tell you what it felt like to be there.

cards.title: Who watches over the machines that clean a town’s water?
cards.summary: A water plant operator pays attention to the machines and tests that are part of treating water. At a drinking water plant, the goal is to prepare water before it travels through pipes to the people using it.

cards.title: Who works on an ambulance crew?
cards.summary: Emergency medical technicians and paramedics are trained workers who can care for people at an emergency. An ambulance crew may need to find out what happened, bring equipment from the ambulance, and decide how to move someone who needs further care.

cards.title: Who wrote The Wonderful Wizard of Oz?
cards.summary: L. Frank Baum wrote a story about Dorothy, a girl who travels from Kansas to the made-up Land of Oz.

cards.title: Why a clear daytime sky looks blue
cards.summary: Sunlight contains many colors. As it passes through the atmosphere, tiny molecules of gas send some of its light in new directions.

cards.title: Why a push comes with a push back
cards.summary: If you push your hands against a wall, the wall pushes back on your hands just as hard. Every push or pull between two objects works in both directions.

cards.title: Why a ramp makes lifting easier
cards.summary: A ramp gives you a longer path to a higher place. If you lifted a box straight up, you would have to support its full weight while lifting.

cards.title: Why a screw moves forward when turned
cards.summary: A screw has a spiral ridge called a thread around it. Turning the screw is like moving along a ramp that has been wrapped around a rod.

cards.title: Why a seat belt makes stopping safer
cards.summary: When a moving car slows suddenly, the people inside are still moving forward until a force slows them too. A seat belt connects the rider to the vehicle so they slow down along with the car.

cards.title: Why a spacecraft flew through the Sun’s outer atmosphere
cards.summary: The Parker Solar Probe was built to study the Sun from closer than any earlier spacecraft. Its wide heat shield stays pointed toward the Sun, keeping much of the direct radiation off the instruments behind it.

cards.title: Why a spoon handle gets warm
cards.summary: Put a metal spoon in something warm and, after a while, you may feel the handle warm up too. The warm end gives energy to nearby parts of the metal.

cards.title: Why airplanes change the shape of their wings
cards.summary: If you look out at a plane’s wing near landing, parts along the back may slide out or tilt down. These parts are called flaps.

cards.title: Why airports have traffic control towers
cards.summary: Many airports have tall towers where controllers can look out at the runways and paths between gates. They talk with pilots and help keep aircraft apart while airplanes land, take off or move on the ground.

cards.title: Why are beans useful in meals?
cards.summary: Many of the beans people eat are seeds that grow in pods. Peas and lentils come from related plants.

cards.title: Why are coast redwoods famous?
cards.summary: Coast redwoods are the tallest living trees known. They grow naturally along a narrow stretch of the Pacific coast in California and a small part of Oregon.

cards.title: Why are coffee beans taken from cherries?
cards.summary: A coffee plant grows small fruits around seeds. People call the ripe fruits coffee cherries because many look rounded and red, like cherries.

cards.title: Why are forest edges different from the middle of a forest?
cards.summary: Where woods meet a field, the trees are open to the sky on one side. There can be more sunlight and wind close to that edge than deeper among the trees.

cards.title: Why are parts of a car designed to bend in a crash?
cards.summary: When a moving car hits something, its motion can stop very quickly. Parts at the front or back can be made to bend and fold in a planned way.

cards.title: Why are raisins smaller than grapes?
cards.summary: A grape carries a lot of water inside it. When it is dried into a raisin, much of that water leaves and the skin wrinkles around the smaller fruit.

cards.title: Why are some bones in a museum dinosaur a copy?
cards.summary: A fossil cast is a copy that preserves the shape of a real fossil. Casting can help a museum show a bone while the original is kept safe in a collection.

cards.title: Why are some Mesa Verde homes tucked under cliffs?
cards.summary: At Mesa Verde in what is now Colorado, Ancestral Pueblo people built homes in openings under overhanging cliffs. A natural rock roof covered some of the living space, so builders could put up stone walls underneath it.

cards.title: Why are some museum rooms dim?
cards.summary: Light helps you see colors and shapes in a museum. Too much light over time can also fade dyes in cloth, paper, or paintings.

cards.title: Why are some numbers called square numbers?
cards.summary: A square number counts the tiles in a square made with just as many rows as columns. A square with four rows of four tiles uses 16 tiles.

cards.title: Why are some Venice streets made of water?
cards.summary: Venice in northeastern Italy grew across many low islands in a lagoon, a partly sheltered area of water near the sea. Waterways between the islands serve as long routes for boats.

cards.title: Why are some volcanic islands lined up?
cards.summary: A hot spot can supply melted rock beneath a moving plate. A volcano may grow above the hot spot until it reaches the ocean surface and makes an island.

cards.title: Why are the dunes at White Sands so white?
cards.summary: White Sands in New Mexico has dunes made mostly from gypsum, a light-colored mineral. Water can dissolve gypsum in nearby mountains, carry it down, and leave crystals behind as the water dries.

cards.title: Why are the Everglades called a river of grass?
cards.summary: In South Florida, fresh water can move slowly across flat land in a broad, shallow sheet. Sawgrass and other plants grow up through it, so parts of the wetland can look more like a prairie than a narrow river.

cards.title: Why are there clay soldiers near an emperor’s tomb?
cards.summary: The First Emperor of Qin had a huge burial site built near what is now Xi’an. People shaped and fired clay figures of soldiers, horses, and other members of his court.

cards.title: Why are there different swimming strokes?
cards.summary: In swimming, a stroke is a pattern of arm and leg movements that moves a swimmer through water. In front crawl, the arms take turns reaching and pulling.

cards.title: Why are there loose stones under many train tracks?
cards.summary: Many railroad tracks rest on short supports laid across the track, called ties or sleepers. The ties sit in a bed of broken stone called ballast.

cards.title: Why are there rows of trees along some fields?
cards.summary: A strong wind can carry loose soil off an open field. Rows of trees or shrubs can slow some of the air moving near the ground on the sheltered side.

cards.title: Why are there so many rock arches in Arches National Park?
cards.summary: In eastern Utah, Arches National Park has many openings through red sandstone. Sandstone is made of grains that have stuck together into rock.

cards.title: Why are there steel bars inside some concrete?
cards.summary: Concrete handles strong squeezes well, but it can crack more easily where a load pulls it apart. Builders can put steel rods inside a concrete beam or slab when they make it.

cards.title: Why are there stone walls around Old Québec?
cards.summary: The older part of Québec City in Canada stands beside the St. Lawrence River.

cards.title: Why be careful with messages from people you just met online?
cards.summary: When you meet someone through a game, you may know their character name and how they play. You may know very little about who they are away from the game.

cards.title: Why bicycles have different gears
cards.summary: A bicycle chain moves between toothed wheels called sprockets. A low gear makes your feet turn the pedals more times for each turn of the rear wheel.

cards.title: Why birds are living dinosaurs
cards.summary: Birds belong to one branch of the dinosaur family. Their early relatives were small, two-legged dinosaurs that lived long before people.

cards.title: Why brakes press against a spinning wheel
cards.summary: In many cars, pressing the brake pedal pushes liquid through narrow tubes or controls a system that does. At a wheel, the pressure makes brake pads press on a spinning metal disc.

cards.title: Why bridge frames are full of triangles
cards.summary: A rectangular frame can lean sideways if its joints are free to turn. Add a diagonal bar, and you split the frame into two triangles.

cards.title: Why build a circle where roads meet?
cards.summary: A modern roundabout sends traffic around a small island so paths join in the same direction. The road bends as it leads toward the center, which helps drivers slow before entering the circle.

cards.title: Why can a beluga turn its head?
cards.summary: Belugas live in Arctic and nearby waters. A young beluga is gray, and most become white as they grow older.

cards.title: Why can a bicycle coast while its pedals stay still?
cards.summary: Many bicycles have a part that lets power move one way from the pedals to the back wheel. It catches when you pedal forward, so the chain can drive the wheel.

cards.title: Why can a bottle opener lift a cap with a small push?
cards.summary: A metal crown cap has bent edges that grip the bottle’s rim. A bottle opener can slip an edge under one side of the cap while another part of the opener rests against it.

cards.title: Why can a box appear in place of a letter on a screen?
cards.summary: A computer can know which letter was typed and still lack a shape to draw it on the screen. The file stores a number code for the letter.

cards.title: Why can a city stay warmer than places nearby?
cards.summary: On a sunny day, streets, roofs, and walls can warm up and hold some of that heat. At night they can release heat slowly, leaving some parts of a city warmer than greener places nearby.

cards.title: Why can a grassland have so few trees?
cards.summary: Grasses cover broad plains in places with a climate that can support them but often limits trees. The amount of rain is one part of the story.

cards.title: Why can a longer ramp be easier to go up?
cards.summary: A ramp connects a lower place to a higher one with a sloping surface. If two ramps reach the same height, the longer one can climb more gradually.

cards.title: Why can a rubbed balloon stick to a wall?
cards.summary: Rub a balloon against some fabrics and a few electrons can move from one surface to the other. That leaves one surface with extra negative charge and the other with less.

cards.title: Why can a rug make a room sound less echoey?
cards.summary: A hard floor reflects much of the sound that reaches it. A rug gives some of the moving air a tangle of fibers and small gaps to pass through.

cards.title: Why can a vector picture grow without getting blocky?
cards.summary: A vector picture can describe a shape by saying where its edges and curves go. A drawing of a blue circle can be saved as the circle’s center, its size, and its color.

cards.title: Why can a woodland wildflower do well before the trees have leaves?
cards.summary: The ground in a leafy forest can get a lot of sunlight in early spring. Most of the tall branches haven't made their new leaves yet.

cards.title: Why can a written Thai vowel appear before the sound it follows?
cards.summary: Thai text normally runs from left to right. Vowels can be drawn around consonants, including to their left, right, above, or below.

cards.title: Why can American holly stay green in winter?
cards.summary: An American holly keeps its tough, waxy leaves through cold weather instead of dropping them all in autumn. The leaves often have pointed teeth along the edge.

cards.title: Why can an envelope have two addresses on it?
cards.summary: One address shows where a letter is meant to go. A return address tells postal workers where it came from.

cards.title: Why can an onion make your eyes water?
cards.summary: A knife breaks many onion cells when it slices through their layers. Materials kept apart in an uncut onion can then mix.

cards.title: Why can baking soda make batter rise?
cards.summary: Baking soda can react with a food acid in wet batter and release carbon dioxide gas. The gas makes little bubbles that take up room.

cards.title: Why can falling rain turn to ice on a branch?
cards.summary: Freezing rain begins with liquid drops. Those drops can cool below water’s usual freezing point without turning solid right away.

cards.title: Why can interest make an amount of money grow?
cards.summary: Interest is extra money paid for using someone else’s money. A bank may pay you interest to hold money in a savings account.

cards.title: Why can lichens grow on bare rocks?
cards.summary: A lichen grows when a fungus lives closely with a partner that can make sugars using light. That partner can be a kind of alga or a kind of tiny living thing called a cyanobacterium.

cards.title: Why can one shaking object make another start to shake?
cards.summary: Think about pushing a swing. If the pushes come at the right moments, the motion can grow.

cards.title: Why can one specimen matter when scientists name a species?
cards.summary: When scientists give a species a scientific name, a specimen or sometimes a group of specimens can help fix what that name refers to. These examples are called type specimens.

cards.title: Why can people still see streets and houses at Pompeii?
cards.summary: Pompeii was a town near Mount Vesuvius in what is now Italy. In 79 CE the volcano erupted, and ash and other material covered the town.

cards.title: Why can plastics feel so different?
cards.summary: A lot of the material in plastic is made from very long molecules. Such molecules may form loose chains or a tighter network.

cards.title: Why can redbud branches turn pink before spring leaves open?
cards.summary: An eastern redbud can look like a bare tree covered with tiny pink beads near the start of spring. Those are flowers opening along the branches before the leaves spread.

cards.title: Why can salt melt ice on a road?
cards.summary: Ordinary water can freeze at a certain temperature, but water with dissolved salt in it can stay liquid below that temperature. Salt on an icy road can dissolve in small amounts of liquid water at the surface and form salty water.

cards.title: Why can soap make a bubble last?
cards.summary: A bubble forms when air stretches a thin liquid film around itself. Water alone usually cannot keep that delicate film from breaking for very long.

cards.title: Why can the ground suddenly sink into a hole?
cards.summary: Rainwater can slowly dissolve some kinds of rock underground, including limestone. The openings can grow as more water passes through.

cards.title: Why can the top of a blazing star flower stalk bloom first?
cards.summary: A dense blazing star carries rows of small purple flower heads along a straight tall stem. In many plants, the heads at the top start to open earlier than the ones below.

cards.title: Why can water flow straight out of a hillside?
cards.summary: A spring is a place where underground water reaches the surface. Rain or melted snow can sink through gaps in soil and rock.

cards.title: Why can water rush away from a beach?
cards.summary: As waves break near a beach, they push water toward land. Some of that water flows back out in a narrow, fast-moving stream called a rip current.

cards.title: Why can you see several colors in one piece of granite?
cards.summary: A polished piece of granite can show pink, white, gray, or dark grains that fit together. The grains are different minerals.

cards.title: Why can your body react before you decide?
cards.summary: Pulling your hand away from a hot surface can happen before you have time to plan to move. Nerves on the skin send a message inward.

cards.title: Why can your shoulder move in so many directions?
cards.summary: At your shoulder, the rounded top of your upper arm bone fits into a socket. Imagine a ball resting in a shallow cup.

cards.title: Why can’t a snapping turtle hide completely in its shell?
cards.summary: A common snapping turtle has a broad shell across its back, but only a small hard area under its body. It cannot tuck all of its head, legs, and tail between those two parts as some other turtles can.

cards.title: Why can’t you hear a bell through empty space?
cards.summary: A bell makes sound by shaking the material around it. In a room, the bell moves nearby air, and that movement can spread as a sound wave.

cards.title: Why comets grow tails
cards.summary: A comet is a small body of ice, dust, and rock that travels around the Sun. When a comet comes into warmer parts of the solar system, some of its ice changes straight into gas.

cards.title: Why dark spots appear on the Sun
cards.summary: Some parts of the Sun are held by strong magnetic fields. Those fields can reduce the motion that normally carries heat up from below.

cards.title: Why did ancient Romans build so many roads?
cards.summary: Roads tied ancient Rome to places across its growing territory. A good road made it easier to move travelers, soldiers, animals, and goods over land.

cards.title: Why did Apollo 15 take a car to the Moon?
cards.summary: Apollo 15 landed on the Moon in 1971. The crew took a small electric vehicle called a lunar rover, so they could visit spots far beyond their landing place.

cards.title: Why did builders carve buildings into cliffs at Petra?
cards.summary: Petra was a trading city of the Nabataeans in what is now Jordan. Tall sandstone cliffs surrounded it.

cards.title: Why did cities grow between the Tigris and Euphrates?
cards.summary: Mesopotamia was a region around the Tigris and Euphrates rivers. In its drier southern lands, people dug channels to bring river water to their fields.

cards.title: Why did Constantinople become an important city?
cards.summary: Constantinople stood beside the Bosporus, a narrow waterway connecting larger seas between Europe and Asia. That position brought ships and trade near the city.

cards.title: Why did countries create the League of Nations?
cards.summary: After the First World War, leaders wanted countries to have a place to talk through disagreements before turning to fighting. The League of Nations began in 1920, with its center in Geneva, Switzerland.

cards.title: Why did countries form the United Nations?
cards.summary: Near the end of the Second World War, delegates from many countries came to San Francisco. They wrote a charter for an organization called the United Nations.

cards.title: Why did Dawn orbit two different worlds in the asteroid belt?
cards.summary: Dawn traveled to Vesta and Ceres, two large worlds in the asteroid belt. Vesta is mostly rocky.

cards.title: Why did delegates meet in Philadelphia in 1787?
cards.summary: After independence, the United States had a national government with limited power. Representatives met in Philadelphia in 1787 to consider changes.

cards.title: Why did Diplodocus have such a long tail?
cards.summary: Diplodocus was a long-necked dinosaur with a tail that narrowed to a thin tip. The tail alone made up a large part of its length.

cards.title: Why did Ed White step outside Gemini 4?
cards.summary: In 1965, astronaut Ed White opened a hatch and moved outside the Gemini 4 spacecraft. He wore a suit that supplied air and protected him from the space around him.

cards.title: Why did Iguanodon have a spike on its thumb?
cards.summary: One finger on an Iguanodon hand ended in an unusual spike. Some early researchers put the spike on the dinosaur’s nose because they had only scattered fossils to work with.

cards.title: Why did Jacob Lawrence tell one history in many paintings?
cards.summary: Jacob Lawrence painted a series about the movement of many Black Americans from the South to other regions of the United States. One picture can show a train station, another a room, another a group waiting for work.

cards.title: Why did Jules Verne write about imagined trips?
cards.summary: French writer Jules Verne told stories about journeys across oceans, around the world, and to places nobody could really visit. In one book travelers ride in an imagined submarine.

cards.title: Why did Juno fly over Jupiter’s poles?
cards.summary: Juno circles Jupiter on a path that passes over the north and south poles. This gave its cameras a view of places that are difficult to see from Earth.

cards.title: Why did Lincoln give a short speech at Gettysburg?
cards.summary: In November 1863, people gathered in Gettysburg, Pennsylvania, to open a cemetery for soldiers who had fought there. After a long speech by another speaker, President Abraham Lincoln spoke briefly.

cards.title: Why did Mansa Musa travel across Africa?
cards.summary: Mansa Musa was a ruler of the Mali Empire. In the 1300s he went on pilgrimage to Mecca, a city important to Muslims.

cards.title: Why did Maya people use more than one calendar?
cards.summary: Maya people kept track of several cycles of time. One calendar counted 365 days.

cards.title: Why did more people begin working in factories?
cards.summary: For a long time, people could spin thread or weave cloth in homes and small workshops. In Britain, larger machines made it possible to gather several parts of this work in one place.

cards.title: Why did one part of Wisconsin keep its steep valleys?
cards.summary: Much of Wisconsin was covered by moving ice during recent ice ages. Part of the southwest was mostly outside those ice sheets.

cards.title: Why did people build the Great Wall of China?
cards.summary: Rulers in different periods built walls, gates, and towers along parts of China’s northern frontier. Walls could slow a raid and guide people toward guarded crossings.

cards.title: Why did people dig a canal across part of Egypt?
cards.summary: The Suez Canal links the Mediterranean Sea with the Red Sea through Egypt. A ship traveling between parts of Europe and Asia can use it rather than going all the way around southern Africa.

cards.title: Why did people listen for the beeps of Sputnik 1?
cards.summary: In October 1957, the Soviet Union sent a small metal ball into orbit around Earth. It was called Sputnik 1 and was the first artificial satellite.

cards.title: Why did people press signs into clay?
cards.summary: In ancient Mesopotamia, people used clay tablets as writing surfaces. A writer used a tool called a stylus to press small wedge shapes into soft clay.

cards.title: Why did protesters dump tea into Boston Harbor?
cards.summary: In 1773, Britain gave one company new ways to sell tea in its American colonies. A tax on the tea still applied.

cards.title: Why did Rosetta travel beside a comet around the Sun?
cards.summary: Rosetta was a European spacecraft that caught up with a comet named 67P. It stayed near the comet for many months.

cards.title: Why did Stegosaurus have plates down its back?
cards.summary: Two rows of tall plates stood along the back of Stegosaurus. The plates were made of bone, but sat in the skin rather than joining the backbone.

cards.title: Why did the Brothers Grimm collect fairy tales?
cards.summary: Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm collected stories in German-speaking Europe and printed versions of many of them. Tales people tell aloud can change a little with each storyteller.

cards.title: Why did the space shuttle have wings?
cards.summary: NASA’s space shuttle rose into the sky with rocket power and worked in orbit as a spacecraft. At the end of a trip, the winged part came back through the air and glided onto a runway.

cards.title: Why did the Supreme Court rule against separate public schools?
cards.summary: In several places, families challenged rules that sent Black and white children to separate public schools. The Supreme Court considered the cases together under the name Brown v.

cards.title: Why did the United States fight a Civil War?
cards.summary: In 1861, a group of Southern states tried to leave the United States and formed the Confederacy. Their leaders wanted to protect slavery, a system that kept people forced to work as property.

cards.title: Why did Timbuktu become a center for books?
cards.summary: Timbuktu grew near a point where desert travelers could connect with routes into West Africa. Markets brought people to the town, and scholars came to teach and study.

cards.title: Why did travelers come to the Tang capital?
cards.summary: During the Tang dynasty, Chang’an was a large capital with ordered streets and busy markets. Officials, traders, and travelers arrived from far apart places.

cards.title: Why did Van Gogh paint several sunflower pictures?
cards.summary: Vincent van Gogh made several paintings of sunflowers in jars and vases. Some use lots of yellow, yet the light and dark yellows still let you pick out the petals, flower heads, and background.

cards.title: Why did Voyager take a record of sounds from Earth?
cards.summary: Each Voyager spacecraft carries a disc with sounds and pictures chosen to show something about Earth. It includes noises from nature, greetings in many languages, and different kinds of music.

cards.title: Why did wolves return to Yellowstone?
cards.summary: Gray wolves once lived in Yellowstone, but people removed them from the park and few remained nearby. In the 1990s, wildlife workers brought wolves from Canada back to the area.

cards.title: Why do American toad eggs look like long strings?
cards.summary: A female American toad can lay many small dark eggs in a long string of clear jelly. The string can settle among plants in shallow water.

cards.title: Why do apple growers join pieces of two trees?
cards.summary: A seed from a favorite apple can grow a tree, but the young tree may make apples with different qualities. Growers often attach a piece from a known apple tree to the roots and lower stem of another one.

cards.title: Why do aspen leaves shake in a small breeze?
cards.summary: Hold a sheet of paper by one edge and it can wobble in a breeze. The roundish leaves of a quaking aspen wobble especially easily because each sits on a leaf stem that is flattened from side to side.

cards.title: Why do astronauts float in orbit?
cards.summary: Earth’s gravity pulls on an orbiting astronaut and the spacecraft around them. Both are falling toward Earth, but both are traveling sideways so fast that Earth’s curved surface keeps dropping away beneath them.

cards.title: Why do birds build nests in so many different places?
cards.summary: Bird nests can sit on the ground, rest in the fork of a tree, or hang like a little bag. A tree cavity can hide a nest, while a hard bank near a river can give another bird room to dig a tunnel.

cards.title: Why do black willows often grow beside water?
cards.summary: A black willow can grow on wet ground along rivers, lakes, and other low places. Like many willows, it makes very small seeds with light hairs that help them float away.

cards.title: Why do blueberry bushes like acidic soil?
cards.summary: Different plants grow best in different kinds of soil. Many blueberries do well in soil that is more acidic than the soil preferred by a lot of other garden crops.

cards.title: Why do brook trout need cool water?
cards.summary: Brook trout often live in cold, clear streams. Cold water can hold more dissolved oxygen than warm water.

cards.title: Why do brown rice and white rice look different?
cards.summary: A rice grain grows inside a hard covering called a hull. A machine takes that outside covering off before the rice is eaten.

cards.title: Why do burdock burs follow you home on your socks?
cards.summary: A dry burdock head has lots of tiny curved tips on its outside. Those tips can catch threads in a sock or grab hairs in an animal's coat.

cards.title: Why do cattails have brown heads that turn fluffy?
cards.summary: A cattail’s tall brown head holds many tiny fruits that carry seeds. When the head breaks apart, they can drift off with a tuft of fine hairs.

cards.title: Why do children lose their first teeth?
cards.summary: A child’s first set of teeth fits into a small jaw. As the jaw grows, many of these teeth have to make room for a later set.

cards.title: Why do clocks show different times in different places?
cards.summary: Earth spins about once a day. When the Sun is high over one part of Earth, another part can be dark.

cards.title: Why do clothespins snap shut when you let go?
cards.summary: A common clothespin has two arms held together by a bent piece of springy wire. The part of the wire in the middle lets the arms turn a little.

cards.title: Why do communities hold festivals?
cards.summary: A festival is a time when people take part in shared events. A community might celebrate a season, honor an important date, or share food, music, and stories.

cards.title: Why do computers send messages in little packets?
cards.summary: A long message can share a busy route more easily if it travels as little pieces called packets. Think of mailing a long story as a series of postcards.

cards.title: Why do computers use 0s and 1s?
cards.summary: A computer can store a tiny piece of information in one of two states. We give those states the names 0 and 1.

cards.title: Why do crews check bridges that people already use?
cards.summary: A bridge inspector looks at the condition of a bridge after it has been built. Parts that were new when it opened can change over time.

cards.title: Why do crystals have neat shapes?
cards.summary: In a crystal, very small particles fit together in a pattern that repeats. Adding more particles in matching positions can grow that same pattern outward.

cards.title: Why do different parts of the US government check one another?
cards.summary: The Constitution gives different kinds of work to Congress, the president, and the courts. It also gives one branch ways to limit or review actions taken by another.

cards.title: Why do distant objects look smaller in pictures?
cards.summary: Stand at one end of a long hallway. The walls get closer together in your view as they get farther away.

cards.title: Why do fables often use talking animals?
cards.summary: A fable is a short story that suggests a lesson. A small mouse in an old fable helps a much larger lion, showing that size does not decide who can be helpful.

cards.title: Why do farmers change crops in a field?
cards.summary: Crop rotation means planning to grow different crops in the same place at different times. If a disease can easily spread among one kind of plant, growing an unrelated plant in that field for a while can leave the disease with fewer plants to infect.

cards.title: Why do flat maps stretch Earth?
cards.summary: The surface of Earth curves, but paper is flat. Any way of drawing that curved surface on a flat page changes something about the places on it.

cards.title: Why do food chains make a web?
cards.summary: A food web shows several paths that food takes through a place. Think of a pond where young insects eat algae.

cards.title: Why do gardeners cover soil with mulch?
cards.summary: A layer of straw, leaves or small wood chips can keep sun and wind from touching bare soil directly. This covering is called mulch.

cards.title: Why do giant pandas eat so much bamboo?
cards.summary: A giant panda spends much of its day finding and chewing bamboo. Its heavy jaws break tough stems, and a special wrist bone sticks out where a thumb might be.

cards.title: Why do governments collect taxes?
cards.summary: Taxes are payments that governments require under their laws. Governments use taxes as one way to pay for things they provide, such as some roads and public parks.

cards.title: Why do hockey players use a puck?
cards.summary: Ice hockey players use curved sticks to move a flat rubber puck across the ice. Its flat face lets it slide, which helps players send it along the surface toward a teammate.

cards.title: Why do Japanese readers learn three kinds of signs?
cards.summary: A sentence in Japanese can use three sets of signs. Kanji are characters that often help show the meaning of a word.

cards.title: Why do jigsaws have edge pieces?
cards.summary: In a rectangular jigsaw, the pieces at the outside have at least one straight edge. That makes them easier to sort before you look for a place for each one.

cards.title: Why do Korean letters fit together in blocks?
cards.summary: Hangul is a way to write Korean. It has letters for sounds, but people arrange the letters in square-like groups.

cards.title: Why do leaves change color in fall?
cards.summary: A summer maple leaf looks green because it has a lot of a substance called chlorophyll. In fall, as days get shorter, the leaf makes less chlorophyll and the green color fades.

cards.title: Why do linguists write sounds with the IPA?
cards.summary: A word’s ordinary spelling does not always tell you how it sounds. In English, the letters “sh” work together in “ship” to spell one sound.

cards.title: Why do little maple “helicopters” spin?
cards.summary: Many maples have dry fruits with a thin wing around or beside a pocket holding a seed. When a fruit falls, the wing can make it turn in the air.

cards.title: Why do little streams join larger rivers?
cards.summary: A tributary is a stream or river that flows into a bigger stream or river. As water runs downhill, small streams often meet and make a larger flow.

cards.title: Why do maidenhair fern leaves look like little fans?
cards.summary: A northern maidenhair fern lifts its greenery on thin dark stems. Look from above and you may see the stems spread sideways instead of sitting in one straight line.

cards.title: Why do mancala games use rows of pits?
cards.summary: Mancala is a family of board games that use small pieces and rows of hollow places. In many versions you pick up all the pieces from a pit, then put them down one at a time in later pits as you go around the board.

cards.title: Why do mangrove trees have roots above water?
cards.summary: Mangroves are trees and shrubs that grow along warm coasts, often where the tide soaks their roots with seawater. Their roots can grow into shapes that support each tree in muddy ground and help some roots get air.

cards.title: Why do many streets have a fire hydrant?
cards.summary: A fire hydrant gives firefighters a place to get water from a supply below or beside the street. In many towns it connects to the same network of water mains that sends water toward buildings.

cards.title: Why do many windows have two layers of glass?
cards.summary: A double-pane window has two sheets of glass with a sealed space between them. The space may hold dry air or another gas.

cards.title: Why do monarch butterflies fly south in autumn?
cards.summary: Many monarchs from eastern parts of North America head south in autumn. They gather in cool mountain forests in central Mexico, where the winter usually lets them survive without laying many eggs.

cards.title: Why do museum exhibits have labels next to objects?
cards.summary: A museum label can tell visitors the name of something, when or where it was made, and why it is in the exhibit. Imagine a smooth lump of stone sitting in a case.

cards.title: Why do museums keep many objects behind the scenes?
cards.summary: A museum often has more objects than it has room to show at once. Staff keep many in storage, where researchers can still study them.

cards.title: Why do oil-based dressings sometimes separate?
cards.summary: Oil and vinegar can look like a single cloudy liquid after you shake a dressing. The motion breaks the oil into drops and spreads them through the watery vinegar.

cards.title: Why do orchards grow more than one kind of apple tree?
cards.summary: Many apple trees grow more fruit when their flowers receive pollen from a different, compatible kind of apple tree. An orchard can have several kinds flowering around the same time to provide that pollen.

cards.title: Why do peanuts grow underground?
cards.summary: A peanut plant makes flowers above ground, but after flowering it grows a slender part that reaches downward. This part is called a peg.

cards.title: Why do people call many routes the Silk Roads?
cards.summary: The Silk Roads were linked routes between parts of Asia and places farther west. Travelers could choose different roads depending on the season, water, or who controlled a pass.

cards.title: Why do people divide up the work of making something?
cards.summary: Imagine making costumes for a class play. One person measures the cloth, one cuts out the shapes, and another stitches them together.

cards.title: Why do people organize information in a spreadsheet?
cards.summary: A spreadsheet is a table of little spaces arranged in rows and columns. One column could name each fruit your class counts, and another could hold how many you saw.

cards.title: Why do people save seeds in seed banks?
cards.summary: A seed bank stores seeds so people can grow their plants again in the future. It may hold many varieties of one crop.

cards.title: Why do people sometimes get money back for returning an empty bottle?
cards.summary: In some places, a drink sold in certain containers costs a little extra because of a deposit. After the drink is gone, someone can return the empty container to a place that accepts it and get the deposit back.

cards.title: Why do people use money?
cards.summary: Money makes it easier to buy and sell things. Imagine you make a hat and want a book.

cards.title: Why do people use the same language in different ways?
cards.summary: A dialect is a form of a language used by a group of people. Their words, pronunciation, or ways of putting words together can differ from another group’s.

cards.title: Why do plants along a stream matter?
cards.summary: The strip of plants beside a stream is called a riparian buffer. It can help both the land and the water.

cards.title: Why do plants have stems?
cards.summary: A stem holds plant parts in places where they can do their jobs. A tall stem can lift leaves toward the light.

cards.title: Why do plants release water vapor?
cards.summary: Water from damp cells inside a leaf can turn into vapor. That vapor escapes through small openings called stomata.

cards.title: Why do products often stop in a warehouse before reaching a store?
cards.summary: A warehouse can gather things that come from different factories or farms. Workers record what has arrived and where it is stored.

cards.title: Why do programs use functions?
cards.summary: A program can give a name to a group of steps it may use again. One name for that group is a function.

cards.title: Why do programs use loops?
cards.summary: A loop tells a program to go through the same group of steps more than once. An animation might use a loop to move a picture a little, show it, and move it again.

cards.title: Why do public buses stop at certain places along a route?
cards.summary: A public bus can follow a route that links neighborhoods and places people want to visit. Instead of stopping everywhere, it has a set of places where riders can usually get on or off.

cards.title: Why do ripe jewelweed pods pop open?
cards.summary: A spotted jewelweed makes orange flowers with darker spots. Later, it grows narrow green seed pods.

cards.title: Why do roads have both yellow and white lines?
cards.summary: Painted lines on a road help people understand how the space is divided. In the United States, a yellow center marking can show where lanes for opposite directions meet.

cards.title: Why do rolled oats look flat?
cards.summary: An oat grain starts inside a tough covering that people remove before cooking it. The edible part left behind is a groat.

cards.title: Why do roof shingles sit partly on top of one another?
cards.summary: Shingles are pieces that cover the surface of many sloping roofs. The lower edge of a piece sits over part of the piece below it.

cards.title: Why do shoots sometimes bend toward a window?
cards.summary: A young stem beside a window can bend as it grows. The side away from the strongest light can stretch more than the lit side.

cards.title: Why do snowflakes usually have six sides?
cards.summary: A snowflake begins when water forms a tiny ice crystal in a cold cloud. Water molecules fit together in a repeating pattern in ice.

cards.title: Why do so many pond plants grow at the edge?
cards.summary: Near a pond’s edge, the water is often shallow enough for sunlight to reach the bottom. Some plants can put roots in the mud and send leaves up to the air.

cards.title: Why do some bridge cables fan out from a tower?
cards.summary: On a cable-stayed bridge, strong cables run from the tower to points on the roadway below. The cables pull on the roadway and help hold it up.

cards.title: Why do some bridges have gaps or metal strips across the roadway?
cards.summary: Many materials get a little longer when they warm up and shorter when they cool. On a long bridge, a small change in each part can add up to noticeable movement.

cards.title: Why do some Buddhist towers have stacked roofs?
cards.summary: A pagoda is a tower found in parts of Asia. In many examples, each level has a wide roof or ledge that makes the tower look like a stack.

cards.title: Why do some buildings have plants on their roofs?
cards.summary: Some roofs are built with a layer for plants to grow in above a waterproof roof. Leaves and the growing layer can catch part of a rain shower.

cards.title: Why do some churches at Lalibela sit below ground level?
cards.summary: In Lalibela in Ethiopia, builders cut churches from rock instead of stacking up separate stones. For some of them, they removed rock from around the walls, leaving the outside in place, then cut rooms inside.

cards.title: Why do some decimal digits repeat forever?
cards.summary: When you divide one by three, the first digit after the decimal point is three. The division leaves a remainder of one in the current place.

cards.title: Why do some doors close slowly on their own?
cards.summary: Some doors have a little box and an arm that move together as the door opens. Opening the door presses on a spring inside the box.

cards.title: Why do some factories and building crews need welders?
cards.summary: A welder joins metal parts so they can work as a larger piece. A factory may need several pieces joined for a frame.

cards.title: Why do some ferns have dots under their leaves?
cards.summary: Turn over a mature leaf on some ferns and you may see rows of round brown spots. The spots are groups of tiny cases that hold spores.

cards.title: Why do some filenames end in .jpg or .txt?
cards.summary: The end of a filename after a dot often tells you what kind of file it is. For example, .jpg commonly names one kind of picture file, and .txt often names plain text.

cards.title: Why do some fireflies flash in patterns?
cards.summary: Some fireflies make short flashes using a light-making part of the body. The number of flashes and the space between them can form a pattern.

cards.title: Why do some forest pools disappear in summer?
cards.summary: A low spot in a forest can collect rain and melted snow and turn into a shallow pool. In some years that same spot dries up by summer.

cards.title: Why do some garden plants need a trellis?
cards.summary: A climbing plant may be good at reaching upward but have a stem too thin to stand high on its own. A frame called a trellis gives the stem or its little climbing parts places to grip.

cards.title: Why do some large buildings stand on long supports hidden underground?
cards.summary: The ground close to the surface may be too soft to support a heavy structure. Long supports below it can help carry the structure’s weight.

cards.title: Why do some orchid flowers have surprising shapes?
cards.summary: Some orchid flowers have a broad part that gives an insect a place to land. Other parts can point into a space the visitor must pass through.

cards.title: Why do some parts of a blue flag iris point up and others droop?
cards.summary: A northern blue flag iris often grows at the wet edge of a pond or marsh. When the flower opens, it has three smaller parts pointing upward and three broader parts that tip outward or downward.

cards.title: Why do some plains hold bunches of steep ravines?
cards.summary: In places called badlands, rain and streams have cut many small, steep valleys into soft layers of rock or dirt. Rain may be rare at times, but a shower can run off quickly where few plants cover the ground.

cards.title: Why do some rice fields look like ponds?
cards.summary: Some farmers place shallow water over a rice field during part of the growing season. Rice can grow in conditions that slow down some weeds, so standing water can help keep a field from getting crowded.

cards.title: Why do some rows curve around the side of a hill?
cards.summary: Water can run quickly down a field if rows lead straight downhill. Planting across the slope makes the rows follow the curves of the hill at about the same height.

cards.title: Why do some soils feel gritty or sticky?
cards.summary: Soil contains mineral pieces of different sizes. Sand has the largest of the three common groups, so it often feels gritty.

cards.title: Why do some sounds seem high and others low?
cards.summary: A sound can seem high or low to your ears. That quality is called pitch.

cards.title: Why do some water drops leave white spots?
cards.summary: As rain or groundwater moves through rocks, it can pick up small amounts of minerals. Water with a lot of dissolved calcium or magnesium is called hard water.

cards.title: Why do some words rhyme?
cards.summary: The words light and kite rhyme because their stressed vowel and the sounds after it match. The spelling can be different, as it is in blue and through.

cards.title: Why do some words sound alike but mean different things?
cards.summary: Think of “pair” and “pear.” In many English accents, both words sound the same. One refers to two things and the other to a fruit.

cards.title: Why do some young caddisflies carry cases made of stones?
cards.summary: Some young caddisflies build a small tube around their soft bodies. They use silk to hold together bits of sand, tiny stones, or pieces of stems found nearby.

cards.title: Why do such small frogs make such loud peeps?
cards.summary: A male spring peeper sends out a high call that can sound like a clear whistle. A pouch of skin under its throat, called a vocal sac, puffs up with air as it calls.

cards.title: Why do the Black Hills stand out from the surrounding plains?
cards.summary: The Black Hills rise like an island of hills and low mountains above the plains of western South Dakota and eastern Wyoming. Long ago, rock was pushed upward.

cards.title: Why do the ends of a staple bend under the paper?
cards.summary: When you press a stapler, a flat piece pushes one staple down through the paper. Its two legs meet small grooves in a hard plate underneath.

cards.title: Why do the Florida Keys form a curved chain?
cards.summary: The Florida Keys are a line of low islands that curves away from the southern end of Florida. Many of the islands are made of limestone left by sea life long ago.

cards.title: Why do the gaps between bricks often make a zigzag pattern?
cards.summary: Look at two rows in many brick walls. The end of one brick is over the middle of a brick below it.

cards.title: Why do the Great Smoky Mountains look smoky?
cards.summary: On the border of North Carolina and Tennessee, high ridges in the Great Smoky Mountains often fade into bluish layers in the distance. Moist air can cool and make tiny water drops that hang in the air as fog.

cards.title: Why do the Outer Banks form long, narrow islands?
cards.summary: The Outer Banks are a series of low islands off North Carolina and a small part of Virginia. Waves and currents move sand along the coast.

cards.title: Why do traditional Mongolian words run down a page?
cards.summary: Traditional Mongolian writing usually goes from the top of a column to the bottom. The next column goes to the right of the one just read.

cards.title: Why do trees stop growing high on some mountains?
cards.summary: As you go up a high mountain, there may be a place where you stop seeing tall trees. This is the alpine treeline.
